scenarios.title: Reading the Code Like a Manual
scenarios.situation: You are handed your first excerpt from the National Electrical Code and told to find the rule that governs working-space clearances in front of an electrical panel. The Code is organized by numbered articles and chapters, and the index points you to Article 110.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most reliable first move when you need to locate a rule in the NEC?
choices: Use the Code's structure — start with the article the index or table of contents points to, then read the surrounding definitions and exceptions.
Memorize the article number now and skip reading; you can guess on the test.
Search the whole book front-to-back until a familiar word appears.
Ask a coworker for their interpretation and write that down as the rule.
scenarios.why: The NEC is a legal reference document, not a narrative textbook: its articles are the map. Article 110 covers requirements for electrical installations generally, and reading the full article — including its exceptions — prevents the classic apprentice error of applying a rule out of context. Speed comes later; accurate navigation is the skill being tested here.
scenarios.hint: Think of the NEC as a filing system, not a story. What tool does a filing system give you first?

scenarios.title: The Interim Credential Question
scenarios.situation: Your apprenticeship coordinator tells you that journeyman hours will take years to accumulate, but the training center offers interim credentials — short certifications like OSHA 10 and First Aid/CPR — that you can earn while your on-the-job hours grow.
scenarios.prompt: Why do interim credentials matter for an apprentice who has not yet qualified for a license?
choices: They document job-ready skills (safety, first response) that employers and programs can verify now, while license-required hours accumulate over time.
They replace the journeyman license, so you can skip the remaining hours.
They are only useful as wall decorations; employers ignore them.
They let you perform work reserved for licensed electricians unsupervised.
scenarios.why: Interim credentials are stackable proof of progress: OSHA 10 shows safety literacy, First Aid/CPR shows site readiness. They never substitute for licensure or required hours, but they keep a learner employable and auditable during the long middle of an apprenticeship — exactly the gap they are designed to bridge.
scenarios.hint: What does an employer need to believe about a first-year apprentice before trusting them on site?

scenarios.title: SQ3R on a Motor Nameplate Manual
scenarios.situation: Your instructor assigns a dense twelve-page motor-controller manual and says you will be tested on it tomorrow. You remember SQ3R: Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review.
scenarios.prompt: Which sequence correctly applies SQ3R to this technical reading task?
choices: Survey the manual's headings and diagrams; turn each heading into a question; read to answer those questions; recite the answers from memory; review the manual again at the end.
Read every page twice, then re-read the hardest page a third time.
Skip to the test-relevant pages and ignore the rest to save time.
Highlight everything, then skim the highlights once before the test.
scenarios.why: SQ3R works because each step has a job: Survey builds the map, Question creates a retrieval target, Read fills it, Recite forces recall (the actual learning event), and Review locks it in. Passive highlighting skips the retrieval step entirely, which is why students who highlight heavily often feel prepared and still blank on the test.
scenarios.hint: Which step is the one where you close the manual and talk to yourself?

scenarios.title: When the Joke Stops Being a Joke
scenarios.situation: A senior journeyman keeps making comments about a coworker's appearance that make the whole crew uncomfortable. The coworker laughs along but later tells you they dread coming to work. You have a harassment-prevention orientation fresh in your memory.
scenarios.prompt: What does the training identify here, and what is the correct response?
choices: This matches hostile work environment harassment — unwelcome conduct severe or pervasive enough to alter work conditions. Laughing along does not make it welcome, and the correct response is to report through the company's procedure.
It is only harassment if the coworker objects out loud; silent discomfort does not count.
It is a personal problem between them; staying out of it is the professional move.
It only counts as harassment if it happens in writing.
scenarios.why: Harassment training centers on two tests: was the conduct unwelcome, and was it severe or pervasive enough to change the work environment? 'They laughed along' is a classic trap — people mask discomfort to survive at work. Reporting channels exist precisely so one apprentice does not have to confront a senior journeyman alone.
scenarios.hint: Ask who the training says decides whether conduct was welcome — the person doing it, or the person receiving it?

scenarios.title: The First Paycheck Plan
scenarios.situation: You land an apprenticeship at $19/hour and want to avoid the debt spiral you have seen other trades workers fall into. Your budgeting module covered the 50/30/20 rule, APR on revolving credit, and the rule that credit utilization under 30% protects your score.
scenarios.prompt: What is the soundest plan for the first three paychecks?
choices: Budget roughly 50% to needs, 30% to wants, 20% to savings/debt; keep credit-card balances below 30% of the limit and pay revolving balances in full to avoid high APR interest.
Put everything on a credit card to build credit fast, then pay the minimums.
Skip the budget — apprentices do not earn enough for budgeting to matter.
Take a payday loan for tools now and sort out the budget after the first raise.
scenarios.why: The 50/30/20 split is a planning scaffold, not a law, but the math it protects is real: revolving credit at high APR compounds against you, and utilization above 30% drags your score down — exactly when a young worker needs credit for a vehicle or tools. Minimum payments keep you in debt for years; full payoff keeps the card working for you instead of the reverse.
scenarios.hint: Which of these plans has you paying interest to a lender, and which has the lender's product working for you?

scenarios.title: Aptitude Test: Algebra Under Pressure
scenarios.situation: The etA aptitude test includes algebra word problems, including Ohm's law applications. One question reads: 'A 240-volt circuit draws 15 amps. The electrician needs the power in watts and must solve for the unknown in P = V × I, then check the answer against a second formula.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the power, and what does the verification step demonstrate?
choices: 3,600 watts; the verification (e.g., P = I²R after solving R = V/I = 16 Ω, giving 15² × 16 = 3,600 W) demonstrates the aptitude-test skill of checking work with an independent method.
255 watts; verification is unnecessary if you trusted the first formula.
360 watts; multiplication of voltage and current gives watt-hours directly.
36,000 watts; decimal placement does not matter on a multiple-choice test.
scenarios.why: P = V × I gives 240 × 15 = 3,600 W. The independent check matters more than the number: solving R = V/I = 16 Ω and confirming I²R = 225 × 16 = 3,600 W catches the classic slip of multiplying 240 × 15 as 3,600 while misplacing a decimal elsewhere. Aptitude tests are designed to reward learners who verify, because field electrical math has no answer key.
scenarios.hint: Can you solve for resistance first, then get power without ever touching P = V × I? If yes, you have a real check.

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Electrician Apprentice as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The Electrician Apprenticeship: etA Entrance Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Electrician Apprenticeship: etA Entrance is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Electrician Apprenticeship: etA Entrance?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Electrician Apprenticeship: etA Entrance issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Electrician Apprenticeship: etA Entrance is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Electrician Apprenticeship: etA Entrance supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Electrician Apprenticeship: etA Entrance failure in Electrician Apprentice.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Electrician Apprenticeship: etA Entrance
evidence: All Electrician Apprenticeship: etA Entrance components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: Trace the Dead Receptacle
scenarios.situation: A bedroom receptacle is dead. The breaker is ON, the panel shows 120V at the breaker terminal, and the rooms on either side have power.
scenarios.prompt: Where is the fault, and what is the next test?
choices: The breaker is bad — replace it; 120V at the terminal means nothing.

The fault is in the branch wiring between the panel and the dead receptacle: voltage is present at the breaker but missing at the device, so walk the branch from the load backward — the next test is voltage at the last working device upstream, then at each box toward the panel, until you find where voltage reappears.
The utility lost a phase — call the power company.
All the receptacles are bad — replace them all.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The boundary is already half-drawn: voltage present at the breaker, missing at the device — so the open is in the branch run between them. Walking backward from the load finds the exact box where voltage reappears, and the fault is between that box and the next dead one.
scenarios.hint: Voltage is present at the start of the branch and missing at the end — what does that tell you about the middle?
objectives: Trace faults by walking the chain

scenarios.title: The Breaker That Keeps Tripping
scenarios.situation: A 20A branch breaker trips every afternoon when the shop's compressor and dust collector run together. It resets fine and holds all morning. Someone suggests swapping in a 30A breaker 'since the wire looks thick enough.'
choices: Refuse the upsize: the breaker is the protection stage correctly reporting a downstream overload (two motor loads exceeding 20A in the afternoon). Diagnose the load side — measure actual current, check whether the loads belong on one circuit — and fix the system (dedicated circuit, load scheduling) instead of silencing the reporter.
The breaker is worn out — replace it with the same 20A and hope.
Tell the shop to run the machines less — the system is fine.
Swap the 30A in — the wire looks like 10 AWG anyway.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. A breaker that holds all morning and trips every afternoon is doing its job: reporting an overload condition. Upsizing the breaker without verifying conductor ampacity and terminations converts a protection device into a fire permit. The systems move is to fix the downstream condition the protection is reporting.
scenarios.hint: Is the breaker broken — or is it the only component telling the truth?
evidence: Trips only when both machines run; holds otherwise

scenarios.title: Follow the Fault Current
scenarios.situation: A drill press frame gives a tingle. Meter shows 60V from frame to a nearby water pipe. The circuit's EGC is intact back to the panel.
scenarios.prompt: Trace the fault current's path — what is it telling you?
choices: The fault current travels frame to EGC to panel ground bar to main bonding jumper to service neutral and back to the source — a tingle instead of a trip means the path has high impedance somewhere (loose EGC splice, corroded bond), so fault current is too small to trip the breaker but large enough to feel. Find and repair the high-impedance joint.
The ground rod is absorbing the fault — drive a second rod.
The 60V is normal induced voltage — ignore it.
The breaker will trip eventually — wait for it.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. An intact-looking EGC with a tingle means the fault path exists but is high-impedance: enough current to raise the frame to 60V, not enough to trip the breaker. The diagnostic is impedance in the fault path — tug-test splices, check bond torque, measure the EGC's continuity under load.
scenarios.hint: If the path were truly low-impedance, what would the breaker have done already?
evidence: Holding — fault current below trip threshold

scenarios.title: Voltage Drop as a System Symptom
scenarios.situation: A table saw 180 feet from the panel bogs down on startup and the shop lights dim. Voltage at the panel stays 120V; voltage at the saw sags to 102V under load.
choices: The saw motor is failing — replace the saw.
The panel is undersized — upgrade the service.
The utility is browning out — file a complaint.

The branch run is the impedance: 180 feet of conductor drops 18V under starting current while the panel holds steady — the symptom lives in the run, not the source or the load. Fix it at the system level: upsize the branch conductors, shorten the run, or add a closer subpanel — not a bigger breaker or a new saw.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Panel steady plus load sagging equals drop in between — the run is the resistor. The systems fix addresses the run's impedance (bigger wire, shorter run, nearer subpanel), because the source and the load are both behaving normally.
scenarios.hint: The panel holds 120V while the saw sees 102V — where did the 18 volts go?
objectives: Distinguish source, run, and load faults
Fix impedance at the system level

scenarios.title: Size the Circuit
scenarios.situation: A 1500W space heater will run on a 120V branch circuit. The existing circuit has 14 AWG wire on a 15A breaker.
scenarios.prompt: Is this safe, and what does Ohm's law say?
choices: I = P/V = 1500/120 = 12.5A — under the 15A breaker and within 14 AWG ampacity; safe for a dedicated circuit, but continuous-load rules (125%) would require 15.6A capacity — a 20A/12 AWG circuit is the correct design
12.5A is fine on 15A — no issues at all
1500W is too much for any residential circuit
Upgrade to 10 AWG immediately — 14 AWG will melt
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The math: 12.5A < 15A breaker, and 14 AWG handles 15A — so it works. But NEC continuous-load rules (heaters run 3+ hours) require sizing at 125%: 12.5 × 1.25 = 15.6A, exceeding the 15A circuit. The professional design is a 20A breaker with 12 AWG. The exam tests both the calculation and the continuous-load rule.
scenarios.hint: What kind of load is a space heater — and what multiplier does the NEC require?

scenarios.title: Diagnose the Dead String
scenarios.situation: Half the recessed lights on a circuit are dead. The dead ones are all downstream of one point. The breaker is fine.
scenarios.prompt: Series or parallel behavior — and where's the fault?
choices: Parallel branch fault: residential lighting is parallel, so a dead group downstream of one point means an open connection at that point — check the last working fixture's downstream splice
Series fault: rewire the whole run in series
Bad breaker — replace it
All the bulbs burned out simultaneously
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Parallel wiring means each fixture gets full voltage independently — a group dead downstream of one point is an open at that point (loose wirenut, failed backstab). The fault-finding logic: in parallel systems, find the boundary between working and dead; the open is there.
scenarios.hint: In parallel wiring, what does 'dead downstream of one point' tell you?
evidence: 4 of 8 fixtures dead, all downstream of fixture #4

scenarios.title: Read the Meter Right
scenarios.situation: An exam question asks for the peak voltage of a nominal 120V residential circuit.
choices: ~170V peak (120 × 1.414); peak-to-peak ~340V — the 120V is RMS, the effective working value
120V — that's what the meter says
240V — residential is 240V
85V — RMS is higher than peak
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Meters read RMS (root mean square) — the DC-equivalent heating value. Peak = RMS × √2 ≈ 170V. This is a classic exam trap testing whether you know what '120V' actually means versus what the sine wave peaks at.
scenarios.hint: What does the meter actually measure — peak or RMS?

scenarios.title: Size the Transformer
scenarios.situation: A shop needs 120V control power from a 480V feed. The control load is 1500VA.
choices: 480V→120V, 1500VA minimum (next standard size up, e.g., 1.5–2 kVA) — turns ratio 4:1, secondary current 12.5A
Any 120V transformer — voltage is all that matters
480V→240V — close enough for controls
1500W of transformers wired in parallel
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Transformers are sized by VA (apparent power): load 1500VA → specify ≥1500VA (next standard size). Turns ratio 480:120 = 4:1. Secondary current = 1500/120 = 12.5A — size secondary conductors for that. VA sizing, not watts, because control loads may have poor power factor.
scenarios.hint: What unit sizes transformers — and what current flows on the secondary?

scenarios.title: Check the Power Bill
scenarios.situation: A motor nameplate: 240V, 10A, power factor 0.8. The owner thinks it uses 2400W.
scenarios.prompt: What is the true power, and why does it matter?
choices: True power = V × I × PF = 240 × 10 × 0.8 = 1920W — the 480W difference is reactive power that loads conductors and transformers without doing work; you size from apparent power (2400VA)
2400W — the owner is right
1920VA — power factor doesn't matter
It uses no power — motors are efficient
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Apparent power (2400VA) is what the conductors and transformer feel; true power (1920W) is what does work. The exam tests this distinction relentlessly: size from VA, bill from W (roughly), and correct power factor with capacitors when needed.
scenarios.hint: What does the wire feel — watts or volt-amps?

scenarios.title: Split the Volt-Amps
scenarios.situation: A 208V single-phase load draws 8A at 0.9 power factor. The apprentice reports 'it uses 1,664 watts.'
choices: 1,664W is correct — volts times amps is watts.
The load uses 1,848W — multiply by 1.11 for single-phase.

Apparent power is 208 x 8 = 1,664 VA, but true power is 1,664 x 0.9 = 1,498W — the apprentice conflated VA with watts. Conductors and transformers feel the full 1,664 VA; only 1,498W does work, and the 166 VAR difference is reactive power the system must still carry.
Power factor does not apply to single-phase loads.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Volts times amps is volt-amps, not watts — watts need the power factor. The exam punishes this conflation relentlessly: size from VA, and only claim watts after multiplying by PF. The apprentice's number is right in magnitude and wrong in meaning.
scenarios.hint: What does the wire feel — the watts, or the volt-amps?

domains.name: NEC Code: Articles That Decide

scenarios.title: Space the Receptacles
scenarios.situation: A 14-foot bedroom wall has a door at one end. The plan shows one receptacle at the far end.
choices: No — the 6/12 rule: no point more than 6 ft from a receptacle; a 14-ft wall needs receptacles so the max spacing is 12 ft — add one (door swings and fixed cabinets don't count as wall space, measured along the floor line)
Yes — one receptacle per wall is enough
Yes — bedrooms are exempt
No — bedrooms need receptacles every 4 feet
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. NEC 210.52(A): receptacles spaced so no point along the floor line is more than 6 ft from one — max 12 ft apart. A 14-ft wall with one receptacle at the end leaves points >6 ft away. The exam loves the 6/12 rule with doors and breaks.
scenarios.hint: Measure along the floor line: how far is the worst point from the receptacle?
evidence: 14-ft wall, door at one end, one receptacle at far end

scenarios.title: Protect the Bedroom
scenarios.situation: A bedroom remodel adds receptacles. The existing circuit has no AFCI. The panel is full.
choices: AFCI protection for the bedroom branch circuit — use a dual-function AFCI/GFCI breaker if the panel accepts tandem/dual breakers, or an AFCI dead-front/device at the first outlet; the remodel triggers the requirement
Nothing — existing circuits are grandfathered forever
GFCI only — bedrooms need GFCI not AFCI
Rewire the whole house
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. NEC 210.12 requires AFCI for dwelling-unit living areas including bedrooms; modifications/extensions trigger compliance. Options: dual-function breaker, or AFCI protection at the first outlet (406.4(D)(4) style rules). Grandfathering doesn't cover new work.
scenarios.hint: Does new work in the bedroom trigger current AFCI rules?

scenarios.title: Find the Violation
scenarios.situation: Inspection finds neutral bonded to ground in a subpanel. The installer says 'more grounding is safer.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the violation and the danger?
choices: NEC 250.24(A)(5) / 250.142: neutral-ground bond belongs ONLY at the service — downstream bonds create parallel neutral paths, energizing EGCs and metal parts with neutral current; remove the subpanel bond
No violation — more grounding is indeed safer
Minor issue — note it and move on
Violation, but the danger is only theoretical
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Downstream N-G bonds split neutral current onto grounding paths — metal conduit and equipment cases carry current continuously, creating shock and fire risk. 'More grounding' confuses bonding with safety; the single bonding point is what makes fault clearing work.
scenarios.hint: Where does neutral current go when there are two N-G bonds?

scenarios.title: Derate the Conduit
scenarios.situation: Six current-carrying 12 AWG THHN conductors in one conduit, 35°C ambient. The load is 18A per conductor.
choices: Base 30A (90°C) × 0.80 (4-6 CCC) × 0.94 (35°C) = 22.6A → capped by 75°C terminations and 240.4(D) at 20A; 18A load complies with margin
30A base — no derating needed
12 AWG is always 20A — derating doesn't apply
Fails — must upsize to 10 AWG
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The workflow: start at 90°C for derating math (30A), apply adjustment factors (0.80 fill × 0.94 temp = 22.6A), then cap at the lowest termination rating and 240.4(D)'s 20A limit for 12 AWG. 18A < 20A complies. Skipping any step is the exam trap.
scenarios.hint: Walk the four-step ampacity workflow — where does each number come from?

scenarios.title: Size the Service
scenarios.situation: Dwelling: 2000 sq ft, standard appliances, no electric heat. Rough service size?
scenarios.prompt: Using the NEC Article 220 standard method at a high level, what service is indicated?
choices: General lighting: 2000 × 3VA = 6000VA; small-appliance 2×1500 + laundry 1500 = 4500VA; first 10kVA at 100%, remainder at 40% → demand ≈ 10,200VA + range/dryer at nameplate; total lands near 100A → 100A minimum service, 200A the modern standard recommendation
60A — dwellings need little power
400A — always max it out
50A per 1000 sq ft = 100A exactly, no calculation needed
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Article 220's standard method: 3VA/sq ft general lighting, SABC/laundry allowances, demand factors (100% first 10kVA, 40% remainder), plus major appliances at nameplate/demand. The math lands ~100A minimum; 200A is the professional recommendation for headroom and future loads (EV, etc.).
scenarios.hint: What does Article 220 count, and what do demand factors do to the total?
evidence: 2000 sq ft, gas heat, standard appliances

scenarios.title: Feed the Kitchen
scenarios.situation: A dwelling kitchen has a refrigerator, a microwave, and countertop receptacles all planned on one 20A circuit.
choices: One 20A circuit is fine — kitchens are just rooms.
Kitchens need no small-appliance circuits if the appliances are gas.

Two 20A small-appliance branch circuits minimum for the kitchen (plus dedicated circuits as needed): 210.52(B) requires at least two SABCs serving countertop receptacles, and loading the fridge, microwave, and counters onto one 20A circuit guarantees nuisance trips and a failed inspection — the microwave alone wants its own circuit in practice.
Every receptacle needs its own 20A circuit.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. 210.52(B) demands two 20A SABCs for dwelling kitchens, and one 20A circuit for fridge plus microwave plus counters is a design failure the inspector will catch.
scenarios.hint: How many small-appliance circuits does the Code demand in a kitchen — and what happens when the microwave starts?

domains.name: Wiring Methods: Raceways, Cables, Boxes, Devices

scenarios.title: Pick the Raceway
scenarios.situation: An underground feeder runs beneath a parking lot to a detached garage. Physical damage is possible where it emerges.
scenarios.prompt: What is the code-compliant wiring method?
choices: PVC underground with RMC (or Schedule 80 PVC) for the emergence/riser where subject to physical damage — 300.5(D)(4) requires protection; PVC alone at the riser fails
EMT the whole way — cheap and easy
Direct-burial NM cable
PVC everywhere including the exposed riser
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Underground: PVC is fine buried. But where the raceway emerges and is subject to physical damage, 300.5(D)(4) requires Schedule 80 PVC, RMC, or IMC. EMT underground corrodes; NM can't be buried; unprotected PVC risers get hit. The exam tests the transition point.
scenarios.hint: What happens at the emergence point — and what does 300.5 require there?
evidence: Under parking lot, emerging at garage

scenarios.title: Reject the Cable
scenarios.situation: A contractor ran NM cable exposed along a warehouse wall to feed receptacles. It's neat and stapled.
choices: 334.12 / 334.15: NM not permitted where exposed to physical damage or in commercial/industrial occupancies as described — warehouse walls need protection or MC/conduit; neatness doesn't cure the violation
No violation — neat work is compliant
Violation only if over 600V
NM is fine in warehouses
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. NM's permitted uses (334.10) are dwelling-centric; 334.12/15 restrict exposed work and damage-prone locations. Warehouses = physical damage risk = NM prohibited. MC cable or conduit is the fix. The exam repeatedly tests NM's boundaries.
scenarios.hint: What does 334 say about NM in this occupancy and exposure?

scenarios.title: Count the Box
scenarios.situation: Box contains: 3× 12-2 NM cables, 1 duplex receptacle, internal cable clamps.
scenarios.prompt: What minimum box volume is required?
choices: Conductors 6 + grounds 1 + device 2 + clamps 1 = 10 × 2.25 cu in = 22.5 cu in minimum
6 conductors × 2.25 = 13.5 cu in
Count only the hots: 3 × 2.25 = 6.75 cu in
Any standard box — fill rules are guidelines
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. 314.16 count: 6 current-carrying (3 black + 3 white) = 6, all grounds = 1, device = 2, internal clamps = 1 → 10 volumes × 2.25 (12 AWG) = 22.5 cu in. Forgetting device=2 or counting grounds per-wire are the classic errors.
scenarios.hint: How many volumes does the device count? The grounds?

scenarios.title: Wire the Stairwell
scenarios.situation: A stairwell light needs control from top and bottom. Power enters at the bottom switch box.
choices: 3-way circuit: power hot to common of SW1 (bottom), two travelers to SW2 (top), common of SW2 to the light — either switch toggles by rerouting the traveler path
Two single-pole switches in series
Two single-pole switches in parallel
One 3-way switch is enough
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Two-location control requires two 3-way switches with travelers between; commons carry power-in and load-out. Series single-poles would require both ON; parallel gives OR logic but isn't the standard method. The exam tests traveler logic relentlessly.
scenarios.hint: What do the travelers do — and which terminals are the commons?

scenarios.title: Protect the Circuit
scenarios.situation: Kitchen counter receptacles: the GFCI is wired with downstream receptacles on the LINE terminals.
scenarios.prompt: What is the consequence and fix?
choices: Downstream receptacles are NOT GFCI-protected — move them to LOAD terminals (with line/load correctly identified) so a ground fault downstream trips the GFCI; test with the TEST button
No consequence — LINE and LOAD are interchangeable
The GFCI itself won't work
Replace all receptacles with GFCI type
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. GFCI LINE terminals feed the device itself; LOAD terminals extend protection downstream. Landing downstream on LINE leaves them unprotected — the most common GFCI wiring error. Fix: identify line (feed) vs load (downstream) with a meter, land correctly, test.
scenarios.hint: What do LOAD terminals do that LINE terminals don't?
evidence: TEST button trips only the GFCI itself

scenarios.title: Fill the Conduit
scenarios.situation: Four 12 AWG THHN conductors (plus one 12 AWG ground) in 1/2-inch EMT. The apprentice says 'five wires, that is too many.'
choices: No — five wires max out 1/2-inch EMT.

Yes: Chapter 9 Table 4 gives 1/2-inch EMT 0.122 sq in at 40 percent fill (more than two wires); Table 5 gives 12 AWG THHN 0.0133 sq in each — five conductors x 0.0133 = 0.0665 sq in, well under 0.122. Count the ground in fill (it occupies space) but not as a current-carrying conductor for derating.
Yes — conduit fill rules do not apply to EMT.
No — grounds never count in fill, so it is four wires and still too many.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Conduit fill is area arithmetic: Table 4 for the raceway at the right fill percentage (40 percent for 3+ wires), Table 5 for each conductor's area, sum and compare. The ground counts for fill but not for derating — the two most confused rules in wiring methods, kept straight here.
scenarios.hint: What two tables do you need — and does the ground count for fill, derating, or both?

domains.summary: Conduit systems, cable assemblies, box fill, switches and receptacles — the physical craft.

domains.name: Motors and Controls: Article 430

scenarios.title: Pull the Right Current
scenarios.situation: You need the full-load current for a 7.5 HP, 208V, 3-phase motor for a plan review.
choices: Table 430.250 — the NEC mandates table values for motor calculations, not HP×746/V theory
Compute: 7.5 × 746 / (208 × 1.73) — theory is fine
Ask the manufacturer
Use 10A per HP as a rule of thumb
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Article 430 requires Table 430.247-250 values — the tables account for real motor efficiency and power factor that theory ignores. Computing from HP gives a wrong number the inspector will reject. This is pure code procedure: tables, not theory.
scenarios.hint: What does Article 430 say about where FLA comes from?

scenarios.title: Build the Control
scenarios.situation: A conveyor motor must NOT restart automatically after a power outage — workers could be inside.
choices: Three-wire (momentary start/stop with seal-in): power loss drops the contactor, and it stays off until someone deliberately presses START — the safe choice for machinery
Two-wire maintained switch — simpler
Direct across-the-line with no control
VFD only — drives handle safety
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Three-wire control's seal-in drops out on power loss and requires deliberate restart — that's the anti-restart safety. Two-wire maintained contacts re-close when power returns, restarting machinery with people inside. The exam frames this as a safety question, and it is one.
scenarios.hint: What happens to each scheme when power returns after an outage?

scenarios.title: Coordinate Protection
scenarios.situation: A 25A FLA motor (SF 1.15) keeps tripping its 30A breaker on startup.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong and what is the fix?
choices: Breaker undersized for inrush: 430.52 allows up to 250% of FLA (62.5A → 60A breaker) for starting current; the 30A was sized like a non-motor load — upsize the branch breaker, keep the overload at ~28.75A for running protection
The motor is bad — replace it
Add a bigger overload relay
Reduce the load on the motor
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Motors draw ~6× FLA at startup; a 30A breaker (120% of FLA) can't survive inrush. 430.52 specifically permits oversized branch-circuit protection (up to 250%) because the overload relay — not the breaker — protects against running overload. Two devices, two jobs.
scenarios.hint: Which device handles starting current, and which handles running overload?

scenarios.title: Justify the Drive
scenarios.situation: A 25 HP supply fan runs 24/7 at constant speed. Management asks if a VFD is worth it — the fan could run at 75% speed most hours.
choices: Affinity laws: power ∝ speed³ — at 75% speed, power ≈ 25 × 0.75³ ≈ 10.5 HP, saving ~58% of fan energy during reduced-speed hours; the VFD typically pays back in 1-2 years on 24/7 variable loads
VFDs don't save energy — motors use what they use
Only worth it above 100 HP
Slowing the fan reduces airflow too much to matter
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The cube law is the whole business case: small speed reductions yield large power cuts. 25→10.5 HP during 75%-speed hours, on a 24/7 fan, is enormous annual savings. The exam tests whether you can run the affinity math, not just recite it.
scenarios.hint: What does the cube law do to a 25% speed reduction?

scenarios.title: Diagnose the Hum
scenarios.situation: A 3-phase motor hums loudly but won't start. It was running fine yesterday. Single-phase test: it starts with a spin assist.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely fault?
choices: Lost phase (single-phasing): one supply phase is open (blown fuse, loose connection) — the motor can't develop starting torque on two phases; check all three phases at the starter with a meter
Bad bearings — replace the motor
Wrong voltage — rewire the motor
Overload tripped — reset it
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Humming without starting + starts with assist = single-phasing: the rotating field needs all three phases to start. A blown fuse or loose connection on one phase is the classic cause. Running single-phased overheats motors fast — find the open phase before the windings cook.
scenarios.hint: What does a 3-phase motor need to start that it can partly do without once running?

scenarios.title: Set the Overload
scenarios.situation: A motor with a 20A full-load current and a 1.15 service factor keeps nuisance-tripping its overload relay, set at 20A.
choices: Size the overload at 125 percent of FLA for a 1.15 service factor motor (430.32(A)(1)): 20 x 1.25 = 25A trip rating. The 20A setting trips on normal running current near full load; the Code anticipates this with the SF-based sizing — the overload protects against sustained overcurrent, not against the motor doing its rated job.
Set it at 30A — bigger is safer for motors.
Remove the overload — the breaker protects the motor.
Set the overload at 20A — FLA is FLA.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Overload sizing follows the service factor: 125 percent for 1.15 SF, 115 percent for 1.0 SF. Setting at FLA guarantees nuisance trips whenever the motor works hard — which reads as a motor problem but is a settings problem. The breaker handles faults; the overload handles overloads; each must be sized to its own job.
scenarios.hint: What is the overload's job — and what percentage of FLA does the Code assign it for this motor?
evidence: 20A FLA, 1.15 SF; overload set at 20A, nuisance trips

domains.summary: Motor theory, starters and control circuits, overcurrent coordination, VFDs — the exam's heaviest article.

domains.name: Electrical Safety: 70E, LOTO, and Survival

scenarios.title: Respect the Current
scenarios.situation: An apprentice says 120V is 'low voltage' and works a live receptacle with no gloves, dry hands, standing on a dry wood floor.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct safety correction?
choices: 120V kills through complacency: wet or broken skin drops resistance to ~1000Ω → 120mA, well into fibrillation range — de-energize and LOTO; 'low voltage' is a lethality myth, and conditions change resistance unpredictably
It's fine — dry conditions make 120V safe
Gloves are optional for 120V
Only high voltage needs LOTO
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Shock math: current = voltage ÷ resistance, and resistance is the variable — sweat, cuts, or concrete floors collapse it. 120V kills more workers than high voltage precisely because it's disrespected. De-energize first; the 'low voltage' framing is the hazard.
scenarios.hint: What variable turns 120V from tingle to lethal?
evidence: Dry now; sweat and concrete later

scenarios.title: Lock It Right
scenarios.situation: You lock out a motor disconnect, but the motor has a VFD with DC bus capacitors and a pneumatic brake.
choices: Beyond the disconnect lock: wait for/dissipate DC bus capacitors (verify <50V), bleed pneumatic pressure, block the brake mechanism — then try-start and test dead; stored energy ignores your lock
The disconnect lock is enough — LOTO complete
Just tag it — locks are for big equipment
Have someone watch the disconnect instead
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. LOTO covers ALL energy: electrical (including stored DC bus charge), pneumatic, mechanical spring/gravity. Capacitors hold lethal charge minutes after lockout; pneumatic brakes can release. Verify zero energy on every form — the lock is necessary but not sufficient.
scenarios.hint: What energy remains after the disconnect opens?

scenarios.title: Read the Label
scenarios.situation: A panel label reads: Arc flash 8 cal/cm², limited approach 3.5 ft, restricted 1 ft. You need to reset a tripped breaker.
choices: 8 cal/cm² requires arc-rated PPE (Category 2 range: 8 cal clothing, face protection) — and even for a 'simple' reset, the restricted boundary (1 ft) demands qualification; de-energize if possible, suit up if not
Just flip it quickly — resetting is low risk
No PPE needed for breakers
Stand 10 feet back and use a stick
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The label is the law: 8 cal/cm² sets the PPE, approach boundaries set who gets how close. 'Just flipping a breaker' has killed — breakers trip for reasons, and reclosing into a fault is an arc-flash event. De-energize first is still the hierarchy's top choice.
scenarios.hint: What do the cal rating and boundaries each tell you?

scenarios.title: Power the Site
scenarios.situation: A construction site runs temp power: 100 ft of extension cords, no GFCI, cords across walkways, one cord repaired with tape.
choices: 1926.404(b)(1): GFCI or assured grounding required on 125V temp receptacles; cords across walkways need protection/elevation; taped repairs fail the daily-inspection standard — temp power is the inspector's first stop for a reason
No violations — temp power is unregulated
Only the taped cord is a problem
GFCI is optional outdoors
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. OSHA 1926 Subpart K specifically targets temp power: GFCI (or assured grounding program) is mandatory, cords need protection from damage, and damaged cords get removed — not taped. Temp power kills disproportionately; that's why it's inspected first.
scenarios.hint: What does Subpart K require for 125V temp receptacles?
evidence: No GFCI, cords across walkway, taped repair

scenarios.title: Trust the Gloves?
scenarios.situation: Your Class 0 gloves are 8 months past their test date. They look fine. You need to work in a live 480V panel.
choices: Don't use them — rubber degrades invisibly and test intervals (6 months for Class 0) exist because look-fine gloves fail; get tested gloves or de-energize the panel — and in a live 480V panel, the whole job needs an energized-work justification anyway
They look fine — use them
Use them but be extra careful
Wear two pairs to be safe
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Insulating rubber degrades from ozone, UV, and age invisibly — the 6-month test interval is the control, not visual inspection. Plus NFPA 70E: live 480V work needs justification, planning, and full protection regardless. 'Looks fine' is how the accident report starts.
scenarios.hint: What degrades invisibly in rubber gloves — and what controls it?

scenarios.title: Read the Arc-Flash Label
scenarios.situation: A panel label reads 'Incident energy: 8 cal/cm2 at 18 inches.' The apprentice grabs standard cotton coveralls, saying 'it is just a panel.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct PPE decision?
choices: Cotton coveralls are fine — 8 cal is low.
No PPE needed for just looking at a panel.

PPE must be rated at or above the incident energy: 8 cal/cm2 demands arc-rated clothing with an arc rating of at least 8 cal/cm2 (PPE Category 2 level) plus the required face, hand, and head protection — 'just looking' still exposes you to the arc-flash boundary, and cotton ignites and continues to burn. The label is a measurement, not a suggestion.
Only the foreman needs arc-rated PPE.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Incident energy is the number the PPE system is built around: your arc rating must meet or exceed it, full stop. Cotton is fuel in an arc event — it ignites and keeps burning after the arc ends. The apprentice's 'just a panel' framing is exactly the complacency arc-flash labels exist to defeat.
scenarios.hint: What does 8 cal/cm2 require your clothing to do — and what does cotton do instead?

domains.summary: Shock and arc flash, lockout/tagout, PPE, OSHA jobsite rules — the non-negotiable foundation.

domains.name: Blueprint Reading: Drawings, Symbols, Specs

scenarios.title: Check the Legend
scenarios.situation: You're roughing in switches from a plan. The symbol is 'S' with a subscript you don't recognize.
choices: Check the sheet legend first — symbols and subscripts vary by engineer; the legend defines them for this job; never wire from assumption
Wire it as single-pole — S always means single-pole
Ask the apprentice next to you
Skip it and come back later
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Subscripts change the device (S₃ = 3-way, S₄ = 4-way, S with WP = weatherproof) and the wiring. The legend is the job's dictionary — veterans check it every job. Wiring from assumption creates rework or hazards.
scenarios.hint: What does the subscript change — and where is it defined?
evidence: Defines all symbols for this set

scenarios.title: Trace the Feeder
scenarios.situation: The one-line shows: 400A MDP → 2" conduit, 4#3/0 → 225A Panel LP-1. You need to pull the feeder.
choices: 2-inch conduit with four 3/0 conductors (3 phases + neutral; EGC per 250.122 in addition) — the one-line's segment notes are the pull specification
Three 3/0 conductors — phases only
Whatever fits in 2-inch conduit
4#500 — bigger is safer
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. One-line segment notation (conduit size, conductor count/size) is the design: 4#3/0 = three phases plus neutral, with the EGC sized separately per 250.122. 'Whatever fits' ignores ampacity and fill; oversizing wastes money and may not fit terminations.
scenarios.hint: What does '4#3/0' specify — and what's missing that 250.122 adds?

scenarios.title: Follow the Homerun
scenarios.situation: Six receptacles on a plan have homerun arrows labeled 'LP-1: 2,4'. Two aren't working.
choices: Panel LP-1, breakers 2 and 4 — the homerun ties those receptacles to those breakers; check the breakers, then trace the homerun path for the open
Replace both receptacles
Check the utility service
Rewire all six
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Homerun labels are the troubleshooting index: they map devices to breakers. Start at LP-1 breakers 2/4 (tripped? voltage?), then walk the homerun route. Replacing devices before checking the source wastes time and parts.
scenarios.hint: What does the homerun label tell you that the symbols don't?

scenarios.title: Catch the Revision
scenarios.situation: You've roughed half the floor per revision Δ2. The foreman hands you Δ3 — the panel location moved 20 feet.
choices: Stop, review the Δ3 clouds, assess rework on completed rough-in, RFI any ambiguities the move creates — building from superseded drawings compounds the rework
Finish per Δ2 — you're halfway done
Move the panel yourself without asking
Ignore it — panels are panels
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Revisions cloud changes for a reason: building on superseded drawings creates rip-out. The professional sequence: stop, assess delta impact, quantify rework, RFI ambiguities, then proceed on current documents. 'Almost done' on the wrong revision is the most expensive sentence.
scenarios.hint: What does the delta cloud change — and what did you already build wrong?
evidence: Δ2 in hand, Δ3 issued, panel moved

scenarios.title: Resolve the Conflict
scenarios.situation: Drawings show EMT in a corridor; Division 26 spec requires RMC in corridors. The EMT is cheaper and faster.
choices: The specification — specs override drawings on conflict; install RMC and RFI if you believe it's an error, but don't substitute unilaterally
The drawings — they're more specific
Whichever is cheaper — value engineering
Ask the apprentice
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Contract hierarchy puts specs above drawings on conflicts. Installing EMT against the spec risks rejection and rip-out at your cost. The RFI is the tool: if the spec seems wrong, ask in writing — don't decide unilaterally.
scenarios.hint: In a drawing/spec conflict, which document wins?

scenarios.title: Find It on the Schedule
scenarios.situation: The foreman says 'receptacles in Room 204 are dead — find the circuit.' The panel schedule shows Panel LP-2, circuit 17: 'REC-204, 206' and circuit 19: 'LTG-204.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct first move?
choices: Open every breaker in LP-2 until the receptacles work.
Start rewiring Room 204 — the schedule is probably wrong.
Call the engineer — schedules are never trustworthy.

Go to Panel LP-2, circuit 17: the schedule maps REC-204 to breaker 17, so check that breaker first (tripped? voltage at terminal?), then trace circuit 17's homerun. The panel schedule is the map — 'LTG-204' on 19 is lighting, a different system. Reading the schedule before touching the panel turns a hunt into a walk.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The schedule distinguishes REC from LTG for a reason, and the first move is always the mapped breaker, not random troubleshooting.
scenarios.hint: What does the schedule say feeds Room 204's receptacles — and what feeds its lights?
objectives: Start from the map, not the panel

domains.summary: Legends, one-lines, floor plans, specifications — reading the documents that govern the work.

domains.name: Transformers and Grounding Systems

scenarios.title: Respect the High Leg
scenarios.situation: A 240V high-leg delta panel: someone landed 120V office receptacles on the B phase.
scenarios.prompt: What happens and what is the fix?
choices: B-to-neutral is 208V — the 120V equipment sees 208V and fails/damages; move 120V loads off B phase; B phase conductors must be orange-identified per 110.15/230.56
Nothing — 208V is close enough to 120V
It works but inefficiently
The breaker will trip immediately
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. High-leg (wild leg) B-phase to neutral is 208V by vector math — 120V equipment fed 208V burns. The orange identification exists precisely to prevent this. Fix: relocate 120V loads to A/C phases, verify orange marking.
scenarios.hint: What voltage is B-to-neutral on a high-leg delta — and why is it orange?

scenarios.title: Specify the Electrode
scenarios.situation: New commercial slab building. The engineer spec'd two ground rods. You know better.
scenarios.prompt: What do you propose and why?
choices: Concrete-encased electrode (ufer): 20 ft of #4 rebar/wire in the footing per 250.52(A)(3) — superior (large concrete contact area), nearly free during construction, impossible to retrofit later
Accept the rods — engineer's spec governs
Add a third rod for good measure
Water pipe only
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The ufer is the best electrode (concrete's moisture + huge contact area) and costs almost nothing during footing construction — but can't be added later. Proposing it via RFI is value engineering that improves the job. Two rods are the minimum, not the optimum.
scenarios.hint: When is the ufer cheap — and when is it impossible?
evidence: New slab, footings not yet poured

scenarios.title: Bond the Derived System
scenarios.situation: A 75 kVA transformer steps 480V down to 208Y/120V for a new panel. The installer landed the secondary neutral isolated (no bond).
choices: Separately derived system with no system bonding jumper — 250.30 requires the neutral bonded at the transformer/first disconnect; without it, secondary ground faults have no return path and can't trip protection
Nothing — isolated neutrals are safer
The transformer is too small
Bond it at the main service instead
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. A separately derived system needs its own N-G bond (250.30) — the secondary is a new electrical world that needs its own fault-clearing reference. No bond = ground faults energize cases indefinitely. Bond once, at the source, sized per 250.28/66.
scenarios.hint: Where does secondary fault current return without a bond?
evidence: Ground fault sim: breaker doesn't trip

scenarios.title: Protect the Service
scenarios.situation: New 1600A, 480Y/277V service. The engineer omitted ground-fault protection of equipment.
choices: 230.95: GFPE required on 1000A+ solidly-grounded wye services over 150V to ground — max 1200A trip setting, and it must be performance-tested at installation per 230.95(C)
Nothing — GFPE is optional
GFCI receptacles satisfy the requirement
Only required above 4000A
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. 230.95's thresholds (1000A+, >150V to ground, wye) exist because 277V ground faults sustain destructive arcing. GFPE is fire protection (not personnel like GFCI), capped at 1200A pickup, and commissioning-tested. Omitting it is a plan-review rejection.
scenarios.hint: What are the three 230.95 thresholds — and GFCI vs GFPE?

scenarios.title: Drive the Rods
scenarios.situation: Existing building, no ufer, plastic water service. You need a grounding electrode.
choices: Two ground rods, 8 ft, ≥6 ft apart per 250.53(A)(2)/(B) — the second rod satisfies the code without needing the 25-ohm test; bond both into the grounding electrode system
One rod — that's enough
One rod plus a written promise it's under 25 ohms
Skip electrodes — the EGC is enough
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. 250.53(A)(2): a single rod must prove ≤25Ω or get a supplemental rod — driving two rods 6+ feet apart is the standard compliance path that skips the test. The EGC is not an electrode; grounding electrodes and equipment grounding are different systems.
scenarios.hint: What does the second rod buy you under 250.53(A)(2)?

scenarios.title: Spot the High Leg
scenarios.situation: A 240V delta panel has one bus stinger-marked orange. Meter reads 208V from that bus to neutral, 120V from the other two.
scenarios.prompt: What are you looking at, and what is the rule?
choices: A defective panel — all legs should read 120V to neutral.

A high-leg (wild-leg) delta: the orange-marked bus is the high leg at 208V to neutral by design (240V leg-to-leg system with a center-tapped ground). The rule: 110.15 and 408.3(E) require the high leg to be durably marked orange, and 120V loads must never land on it — one 120V receptacle on the high leg sees 208V and dies loudly.
A 208Y/120V wye system — wire it as wye.
Normal single-phase — ignore the orange.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The high leg is intentional: a 240V delta with one winding center-tapped gives 120V on two legs and 208V (the 'wild' leg) on the third. Orange marking is Code-mandated precisely because the 208V-to-neutral leg destroys 120V equipment. The diagnostic is the 208V reading itself — that number only occurs on a high leg.
scenarios.hint: What voltage can only exist on one specific leg of a delta system — and what color must mark it?
objectives: Keep 120V loads off the high leg

domains.summary: Transformer connections, grounding electrodes, separately derived systems, ground-fault protection.

domains.name: Troubleshooting: Find It, Fix It, Prevent It

scenarios.title: Split the Circuit
scenarios.situation: Eight receptacles dead on a 20A circuit. Breaker ON, 120V at the panel lug.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most efficient first test?
choices: Half-split: test voltage at the 4th receptacle — 120V means the fault is in the second half, 0V means the first half; one test eliminates half the circuit
Replace all eight receptacles
Replace the breaker
Pull new wire for the whole run
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Half-splitting is binary search: each midpoint test halves the suspect area. With 120V at the panel, the fault is downstream — the midpoint test tells you which half. Three tests max to isolate among eight devices. Part-swapping without testing is the amateur path.
scenarios.hint: How do you eliminate half the possibilities with one measurement?

scenarios.title: Catch the Floating Neutral
scenarios.situation: Customer: lights flicker, some bulbs burn out fast, voltages read 95V on some receptacles and 145V on others.
choices: Open/lost neutral: without the neutral reference, 120V loads sit in series across 240V and divide voltage by impedance — the seesaw (95/145) is the signature; check neutral connections from service inward immediately (fire/shock risk)
Bad bulbs — replace them all
Utility voltage problem — call the power company first
Overloaded circuit — add more circuits
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The voltage seesaw under load is the lost-neutral fingerprint: loads become series voltage dividers across 240V. It's dangerous — 145V destroys electronics and the floating neutral can energize grounding paths. Check the service neutral first (it's often there), then work inward.
scenarios.hint: What makes two 120V readings add to 240V instead of each being 120V?

scenarios.title: Find the Hot Spot
scenarios.situation: A commercial panel feeds a 40A continuous load. The 50A breaker is warm; one lug is much hotter. Voltage drop under load is 8V on that phase.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fault and fix?
choices: High-resistance connection at the hot lug: resistance heats under load (I²R) and drops voltage — de-energize, clean, retorque to spec (or replace damaged lug/conductor), then verify with thermal scan under load
Undersized breaker — upsize to 60A
Normal heating — 40A continuous runs warm
Harmonic problem — install filters
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Localized heat + voltage drop under load = high-resistance connection at that lug. It passes light-load tests and fails heavy ones — the sneaky fault. I²R heating worsens with thermal cycling until it fails catastrophically. Fix is mechanical: clean, retorque to manufacturer spec, verify.
scenarios.hint: Why is only one lug hot — and why does it get worse?
evidence: 8V drop on that phase under load

scenarios.title: Chase the Short
scenarios.situation: A 20A lighting circuit trips instantly on reset. Megger shows 0.2Ω hot-to-neutral with the circuit de-energized.
choices: Isolate by halves: open the circuit at the midpoint box — if the short persists on the panel side, it's in the first half; if it clears, it's in the second — repeat until the faulted segment is boxed, then inspect for the nail/screw/pinched wire
Keep resetting — it might hold
Upgrade to a 30A breaker so it holds
Replace all the fixtures
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. 0.2Ω hot-neutral is a dead short; resetting into it is arc-flash roulette and upsizing the breaker defeats protection. Half-split isolation on the de-energized circuit boxes the fault efficiently — then the physical inspection (nail through cable is the classic) finds it.
scenarios.hint: Why is resetting into a known short dangerous — and what isolates it fastest?
evidence: Recent drywall work on the circuit route

scenarios.title: Sell the PM Program
scenarios.situation: A facility has had three unplanned outages this year from electrical failures. Management sees PM as cost.
choices: Failure economics: unplanned outages cost 5-10× planned maintenance (downtime, rush parts, collateral damage) — propose annual IR scans + torque + records, priced against one outage; the three failures are the budget justification
PM is optional — run to failure is fine
Just buy spare breakers
Blame the installer
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The business case for PM is arithmetic: unplanned failure costs dwarf planned maintenance, and the facility's own three outages are the data. IR scans catch hot spots months early; torque prevents the loosening cycle; records make it predictive. Professionals prevent; amateurs react.
scenarios.hint: What did the three outages cost versus what PM would have cost?

domains.summary: Half-splitting, meter skills, fault signatures, preventive maintenance — the diagnostic craft.

domains.name: Lighting and Controls

scenarios.title: Spec the Space
scenarios.situation: A boutique clothing store needs lighting. The owner picked cheap 70-CRI LEDs at 5000K because 'bright is bright.'
choices: Retail needs 90+ CRI for accurate color and 3000-3500K for inviting warmth — 5000K/70CRI makes merchandise look gray and the space feel clinical; the lighting sells the clothes
Approve — bright is bright
Go brighter: 6500K
CRI doesn't matter for clothes
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Retail lighting is merchandising: high CRI renders colors truthfully (returns drop), warm-neutral CCT invites browsing. 5000K/70CRI is a warehouse, not a boutique. The exam tests that lighting serves the space's purpose.
scenarios.hint: What is the lighting selling — lumens, or the merchandise?

scenarios.title: Meet the Energy Code
scenarios.situation: A new office build's lighting plan has no controls — just switches. The inspector will check IECC compliance.
choices: Multi-level controls: occupancy/vacancy sensors, daylight responsive controls in daylit zones, automatic shutoff (time scheduling), and manual dimming — energy codes require layered automatic controls, not just switches
Nothing — switches satisfy the code
Brighter lamps to compensate
A note saying 'occupants will turn lights off'
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. IECC/ASHRAE 90.1 mandate automatic controls: occupancy sensing, daylight harvesting in daylit zones, scheduled shutoff. Switches alone fail inspection. Lighting controls are as code-mandatory as conductor sizing.
scenarios.hint: What does the energy code require beyond a switch?

scenarios.title: Light the Way Out
scenarios.situation: A renovation converted a storage room into an assembly space. The egress path lighting was never upgraded.
choices: 1 foot-candle average on the egress path (NFPA 101/IBC), 90-minute battery backup (UL 924) with monthly/annual tests, illuminated exit signs, and emergency circuits separated per 700.10
A flashlight by the door
The existing lighting is fine
Exit signs only — path lighting is optional
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Assembly occupancy raises the life-safety bar: metered egress illumination, 90-minute emergency power with documented testing, always-lit exit signs, and separated emergency wiring. Storage-room lighting doesn't cover assembly egress.
scenarios.hint: What changes when the occupancy changes to assembly?

scenarios.title: Kill the Flicker
scenarios.situation: LED retrofits flicker on existing TRIAC dimmers. The client blames the lamps.
scenarios.prompt: What is the actual diagnosis and fix?
choices: Dimmer/driver incompatibility: legacy phase-cut dimmers often mismatch LED drivers — check the lamp manufacturer's compatible-dimmer list; replace dimmers with listed LED-compatible models (or switch to 0-10V/DALI for new work)
Bad lamps — replace them all
Flicker is normal for LEDs
Remove the dimmers entirely
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. LED flicker on old dimmers is the industry's #1 compatibility callback: TRIAC dimmers chop the waveform in ways LED drivers handle inconsistently. The manufacturer's compatibility list is the authority — matched pairs work, mismatched pairs flicker.
scenarios.hint: What does the dimmer do to the waveform — and what does the driver expect?

scenarios.title: Harvest the Daylight
scenarios.situation: A perimeter office row sits under 8-foot windows. The lights burn at full all day. The energy bill is high.
choices: Daylight harvesting: photosensors dim the perimeter fixtures as daylight rises — open-loop or closed-loop sensors with dimming ballasts/drivers; the exam's favorite energy-control measure
More windows
Remove the fixtures
Tell occupants to use the switches
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Daylight zones near windows are code-required control zones: photosensors modulate electric light against available daylight, typically saving 30-60% in perimeter energy. Manual switching never achieves it — automation does.
scenarios.hint: What varies through the day that the lighting should follow?
evidence: Perimeter row, 8-ft windows, full-burn all day

domains.name: Journeyman Exam Day Mastery

scenarios.title: Budget the Clock
scenarios.situation: The exam: 80 questions, 4 hours, open book. You have spent 6 minutes wrestling one calculation and you are only on question 9.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct tactical move?
choices: Keep going — you have already invested 6 minutes and the answer is close.
Skip the exam's calculation questions entirely; they are too slow.

Mark it, move on, and trust the three-pass method: at 3 minutes per question you are already double the budget, and every minute stolen from easy questions you have not reached yet lowers your score more than one hard question raises it. Return in pass 2 with fresh eyes.
Ask the proctor for extra time.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Time budget is 180 seconds per question: at 6 minutes you are spending two questions' budget on one. The three-pass method exists for exactly this moment — bank the easy points first, then spend remaining time where it earns the most. Sunk minutes are gone; future minutes are spendable.
scenarios.hint: How many questions' worth of time have you spent — and what have you bought with it?
evidence: Q9 at 54 minutes — 18 minutes behind pace

scenarios.title: Run the Shortcut
scenarios.situation: Question: 'A 10 HP, 208V, 3-phase motor draws how many amps per Table 430.250?' The answers are close together and the clock is running.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fastest reliable path to the answer?
choices: Compute from horsepower theory: 10 x 746 / (208 x 1.73) — it is faster than finding the table.
Guess the middle answer; table questions are coin flips anyway.
Skip it and come back after the non-table questions.
Go straight to Table 430.250 — the exam expects table values, theory gives the wrong number, and tabbed tables beat derived math on both speed and accuracy. Read 30.8A for 10 HP at 208V directly.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Article 430 mandates table values, and the table is faster than the formula: one lookup versus a multi-step calculation that yields a theoretically-derived wrong answer anyway. This is the exam-day-mastery principle in miniature — know which tool the test wants, and reach for it first.
scenarios.hint: What does Article 430 say about where motor current comes from — theory or tables?

scenarios.title: Win the Lookup Race
scenarios.situation: Question: 'AFCI protection is required in which dwelling-unit locations?' You know it is Article 210, but the clock is ticking.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fastest lookup sequence?
choices: Index first: 'Arc-fault circuit-interrupter' points to 210.12 — one index hit, one section read. The index is the exam's fastest tool for 'which locations' questions; article-tabbing gets you to the neighborhood, the index gets you to the door.
Search your memory for the exact section number and hope.
Flip randomly through the tabs until something looks right.
Start at Article 100 definitions and read forward through Article 210.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The lookup hierarchy on exam day is: tabbed article (neighborhood), then index (exact address), then read the section including exceptions. Starting at definitions and reading forward burns minutes you do not have; the index exists precisely for this question shape.
scenarios.hint: What is faster — reading an article, or asking the index where the answer lives?

scenarios.title: Read the Stem Twice
scenarios.situation: Question: 'Which of the following is NOT required for a service disconnect?' Three answers list real requirements; one lists something plausible but not required. You are rushing.
choices: Answer with the first requirement you recognize — speed matters most.

Read the stem twice and circle the NOT: the question asks for the exception, so the three true statements are the distractors and the false-but-plausible one is the answer. Rushing past a NOT stem is the single most common unforced error on code exams.
Pick the longest answer — longest is usually right.
Skip all NOT questions; they are unfair.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. NOT/EXCEPT stems invert the task: recognition of true statements becomes the trap, because three of them are. The discipline is mechanical — read the stem twice, mark the negation word, and only then evaluate choices. Thirty seconds of care here is worth more than any calculation shortcut.
scenarios.hint: What is the question actually asking for — a requirement, or the absence of one?
evidence: 'Which of the following is NOT required...'

scenarios.title: The Last Ten Minutes
scenarios.situation: Ten minutes remain. Five questions are blank, three are marked for review. Your pace says you can thoughtfully answer about three.
choices: Perfect the three marked reviews; blanks do not count against you anyway.
Stare at the hardest blank until inspiration strikes.
Leave the room early — you have done your best.

Eliminate-and-guess all five blanks first (a blank is a guaranteed zero; an educated guess has positive expected value), then spend remaining minutes on the marked reviews. Never leave a question blank on a no-penalty exam — blanks are the only answers with a 0 percent chance.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Expected-value thinking: a blank scores zero with certainty, while eliminating even one choice raises a guess well above 25 percent. The endgame sequence is blanks first (floor-raising), then reviews (ceiling-raising) — because the cheapest points on the exam are the ones you left on the table.
scenarios.hint: What is the expected score of a blank answer — and of a guess after eliminating one choice?

scenarios.title: Apply the 125 Percent Reflex
scenarios.situation: Question: 'A continuous lighting load draws 16A. What is the minimum branch-circuit rating?'
choices: 16A x 1.25 = 20A: the continuous-load reflex fires before you even reach for the Code — 210.20(A) requires conductors and OCPD sized at 125 percent of continuous loads, so 16 x 1.25 = 20A minimum. On exam day this must be a reflex, not a lookup.
20A — round up to the next standard size.
15A — continuous loads get a discount.
16A — size to the load exactly.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The 125 percent continuous-load rule is the highest-frequency calculation reflex on the journeyman exam: see 'continuous,' multiply by 1.25, then size. Making it a reflex — not a lookup — saves the minutes that table questions will demand.
scenarios.hint: What word in the stem triggers the multiplier — and what is the multiplier?

scenarios.title: Pick the More Complete Answer
scenarios.situation: Two choices both look correct: one says 'install GFCI protection,' the other says 'install GFCI protection at the first receptacle per 406.4(D)(4).'
scenarios.prompt: Which do you choose, and why?
choices: The shorter one — brevity signals confidence.
Neither — if two look right, the question is flawed.

The more complete one: exam answer keys favor the choice that cites the mechanism and the article — 'GFCI protection at the first receptacle per 406.4(D)(4)' is more specific, more verifiable, and matches how code exams are keyed. When two choices agree in direction, pick the one with the precise code path.
Flip a coin; they are equivalent.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Code-exam keys are written from the Code outward: the choice that names the specific section and method is almost always the keyed answer, because it is the one the question writer derived from the article. Specificity is the tiebreaker — vague correctness loses to precise correctness.
scenarios.hint: Which choice could the question writer have copied straight from the Code article?
objectives: Read keys from the Code outward

scenarios.title: The Halftime Check
scenarios.situation: Halftime: 2 hours gone, 34 of 80 questions answered, and you are in the middle of pass 1. The plan was 40 by halftime.
choices: Panic and speed up recklessly — catch up at any cost.
Abandon the plan; plans never survive contact with the exam.
Keep the same pace — 34 is close enough to 40.

Shift gears deliberately: you are 6 questions behind, so tighten pass 1 (30-second rule — if it needs a table or math, mark and move immediately), bank the remaining easy questions fast, and let passes 2 and 3 absorb the marked ones. Adjust the tactic, not the goal — the three-pass structure still works if you enforce the time boxes harder.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. A 15 percent pace deficit is recoverable, but only by tightening the rules that created it: the 30-second mark-and-move rule for pass 1 exists precisely for halftime deficits. Panic wastes the remaining two hours; disciplined acceleration banks the easy points the deficit is currently stealing.
scenarios.hint: Are you behind on questions — or behind on discipline?
evidence: 2 hours, passes 2 and 3 still to come
