domains.name: Solar PV and Battery Storage

scenarios.title: Size the String
scenarios.situation: Ten modules in series, each Voc 40V. The site's record low is -10C, and the temperature correction factor for Voc is 1.14. The inverter's maximum input is 600V DC.
choices: Yes — 10 x 40V = 400V, well under 600V.

Yes, it complies — but only after the mandatory correction: cold raises Voc, so 690.7 requires 10 x 40V x 1.14 = 456V maximum, which is under the 600V inverter limit. The correction step is what the exam checks; the uncorrected 400V math reaches the right verdict for the wrong reason.
No — series strings are never allowed.
Yes — temperature only matters for current.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Cold temperature raises module voltage, and 690.7 requires using the corrected maximum Voc: 10 x 40 x 1.14 = 456V. It complies here (456 < 600), but skipping the correction is the exam trap — on a colder site or a longer string, the uncorrected math passes while the corrected math fails the inverter.
scenarios.hint: Does cold make module voltage go up or down — and what does 690.7 require you to do about it?

scenarios.title: Size the PV Circuit
scenarios.situation: A PV source circuit has an Isc of 8A. Size the conductor and overcurrent protection per 690.8.
choices: 8A — size to the short-circuit current exactly.
10A — round up to the next standard size.
15A — PV circuits always need 15A minimum.

8A x 1.25 = 10A continuous: 690.8 requires PV source-circuit conductors and OCPD sized at 125 percent of Isc (PV is a continuous source), so 10A minimum — then apply the standard next-size-up rules and terminal ratings from there.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. PV output is continuous by nature, so 690.8 applies the familiar 125 percent: 8 x 1.25 = 10A is the floor for both conductor ampacity and OCPD sizing. The exam tests whether you recognize the continuous-load reflex in its PV costume.
scenarios.hint: Is a PV array's output continuous — and what multiplier does that trigger?

scenarios.title: Meet Rapid Shutdown
scenarios.situation: A rooftop residential array: the inspector asks how the system meets rapid shutdown. The installer points to the inverter's AC disconnect.
choices: Yes — the AC disconnect shuts the system down.
Yes — rapid shutdown only applies to ground mounts.

No: 690.12 requires controlled conductors inside the array boundary to drop to 80V or less within 30 seconds of shutdown initiation — an AC disconnect at the inverter does not de-energize the DC conductors on the roof. Module-level electronics (or equivalent listed rapid-shutdown equipment) are the standard compliance path.
No — rapid shutdown was repealed.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Rapid shutdown protects firefighters: the hazard is DC conductors staying live on the roof after the AC disconnect opens. 690.12 demands the array-boundary conductors fall to 80V within 30 seconds — which is why module-level power electronics dominate residential design.
scenarios.hint: After the AC disconnect opens, what is still energized on the roof?
objectives: Distinguish AC disconnect from DC hazard
evidence: Rooftop residential, string inverter, AC disconnect only

scenarios.title: Choose the Inverter
scenarios.situation: A residential roof has a chimney shading part of one roof plane for half the day. Budget is tight but the owner wants maximum production.
choices: The cheapest string inverter — shade does not matter.
A bigger string inverter — oversizing overcomes shade.

Microinverters (or DC optimizers): in a series string, the weakest (shaded) module throttles the entire string, so partial shade punishes string architecture disproportionately — module-level electronics let each module produce independently, recovering the shaded-plane production that a string inverter would lose.
No inverter — wire the array straight to the panel.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Shade on a series string is a weakest-link problem: one shaded module drags every module in the string down to its level. Module-level electronics break the link — each module operates at its own maximum power point. On a partially shaded roof, the architecture decision is worth more than panel wattage.
scenarios.hint: In a series string, what does one shaded module do to its unshaded neighbors?
evidence: Chimney shades part of one plane, half the day

scenarios.title: Size the Battery
scenarios.situation: The owner needs 10 kWh of usable storage nightly. The chosen lithium battery allows 80 percent depth of discharge.
choices: 10 kWh — usable equals nameplate.
8 kWh — multiply by the depth of discharge.

12.5 kWh: usable energy is nameplate x depth of discharge, so nameplate = 10 / 0.80 = 12.5 kWh. Undersizing here means the battery hits its DoD floor nightly and the owner goes dark — the exam tests whether you divide or multiply, and the field tests whether the lights stay on.
20 kWh — always double it.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Depth of discharge is the usable fraction: 10 kWh usable at 80 percent DoD needs 10 / 0.80 = 12.5 kWh nameplate. Multiplying (10 x 0.80 = 8) is the classic inversion error — it sizes the battery smaller exactly when the constraint demands larger.
scenarios.hint: Is usable energy bigger or smaller than nameplate — and which operation gets you from one to the other?

scenarios.title: Interconnect Legally
scenarios.situation: A 40A PV breaker will land in a 200A panel with a 200A main breaker, feeding a residential service.
scenarios.prompt: Does the load-side connection comply with 705.12?
choices: Check the 120 percent rule: busbar rating x 1.20 must cover main + PV breakers — 200 x 1.20 = 240A >= 200 + 40 = 240A, so it complies exactly (and the PV breaker must land at the opposite end from the main). At 241A it would fail — this is the exam's favorite knife-edge calculation.
Yes — 40A is small, so the rule does not apply.
No — the PV breaker must go in a separate panel.
Yes — any breaker size fits anywhere in the panel.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The 120 percent rule (705.12) protects the busbar from being fed from both ends beyond its rating: 1.20 x busbar >= main + PV. Here 240 = 240 complies by the thinnest margin, and the PV breaker must sit opposite the main so no busbar segment carries both currents. One amp over, and it is a supply-side tap or a panel upgrade.
scenarios.hint: What is the busbar's total fed current — and what is 120 percent of its rating?

scenarios.title: Label the System
scenarios.situation: The PV installation is complete and working, but the inspector fails it: no placards, no directory, no rapid-shutdown labels.
choices: Nothing — labels are optional if the system works.
Only the inverter needs a label.
Labels are the installer's choice — inspectors cannot require them.

A permanent directory/placard: 690.56 requires PV systems to be identified with labels showing the system voltages, the locations of disconnects, and rapid-shutdown markings — because the next person to touch the system (firefighter, future electrician) cannot see DC the way they can see AC wiring. Labels are life-safety equipment, not paperwork.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. 690.56 exists for the stranger who meets your system in an emergency: firefighters and future electricians need to know where the DC is, what voltage it carries, and how to shut it down — information a working system does not volunteer. The inspector failed the job because unlabeled PV is a trap for the next person.
scenarios.hint: Who needs to understand this system at 2 AM during a fire — and what tells them?
evidence: Working system, zero labels or placards

scenarios.title: Beat the Shade
scenarios.situation: One module in a 12-module string is shaded by a vent pipe each afternoon, and the whole string's output collapses — not just by one-twelfth.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the entire string suffer, and what are the fixes?
choices: The shaded module is defective — replace it.
The inverter is undersized — upsize it.

Series current must be equal through every module: the shaded module becomes the current bottleneck, throttling all twelve to its reduced output (bypass diodes limit the damage but do not cure it). Fixes: relocate the module, add module-level electronics (microinverters/optimizers), or restring so the shaded module sits with other shaded modules — never leave a lone shaded module in a sunny string.
Shade does not affect output — the monitoring must be wrong.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Series strings are current-matched: every module passes the same current, so the weakest module sets the pace for all. Bypass diodes route around the worst of it, but the string still underperforms badly. The design fixes all attack the mismatch — isolate the shade, not the module.
scenarios.hint: In a series circuit, what must be equal through every component — and who sets that value?

lessons.title: Electrician Apprenticeship: etA Entrance — Core concepts
concepts: Interim credentials (OSHA 10, First Aid/CPR, core craft certifications) document job-ready skills while apprenticeship hours accumulate — they never substitute for licensure.
SQ3R (Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review) turns dense technical documents into retrievable knowledge; the Recite step is where learning actually happens.
Harassment prevention: quid pro quo and hostile work environment are the two legal categories; unwelcomeness is judged from the receiver's side, and reporting procedures protect everyone on the crew.
Core budgeting: the 50/30/20 scaffold, keeping revolving credit utilization under 30%, and paying balances in full to avoid high-APR compounding.
Codes literacy: the NEC is navigated by article structure and index, not memorized; reading exceptions and definitions around a rule is the professional habit.
Algebra readiness: Ohm's law (V = IR) and the power equation (P = VI) are rearrangeable tools — solving for the unknown and verifying with an independent formula is the aptitude-test differentiator.

example.code:
# Ohm's law drill: solve for the unknown, then verify with a second formula
# Given: V = 240 V, I = 15 A. Find P.
P=$(( 240 * 15 ))
echo "P = V x I = $P W"
# Verification: R = V / I = 16 ohm; P = I^2 * R
R=$(( 240 / 15 ))
echo "R = V / I = $R ohm"
echo "Check: P = I^2 x R = $(( 15 * 15 * R )) W"
example.walkthrough: Aptitude-test algebra is about isolating unknowns and cross-checking. Here the primary formula P = V × I gives 3,600 W; solving R = V/I = 16 Ω and confirming P = I²R = 3,600 W proves the arithmetic with an independent path. On a timed test, the 30 seconds spent verifying is cheaper than a careless miss.

pitfalls: Common trap: treating interim credentials as a shortcut to licensure — they document progress; only logged hours plus the license exam qualify you.
Common trap: passive highlighting instead of SQ3R's Recite step — feeling prepared is not the same as retrieving from memory.
Common trap: assuming 'they laughed along' means conduct was welcome — harassment is judged from the receiver's experience and whether it was severe or pervasive.
Common trap: paying only the credit-card minimum — at high APR, minimums service interest first and can keep a balance alive for years.
