lessons.title: Capstone: Residential Service Upgrade Plan — Blueprint
concepts: Your capstone proves integrated capability: Design a complete residential service upgrade: load calculation, panel schedule, branch circuit layout, and NEC-compliant one-line diagram — the portfolio piece that proves job-ready competence.
Scope it in milestones, not monoliths. Each milestone is independently demonstrable — if you run out of time, you still have working pieces.
Document as you build. The artifact plus the write-up is what you show; either alone is half the value.
Build in public where appropriate: version control, clear commits, a README that explains the why, not just the what.

example.code:
CAPSTONE MILESTONES
  1. Perform a dwelling load calculation per NEC Article 220
  2. Size the service, feeders, and grounding electrode system
  3. Lay out branch circuits with AFCI/GFCI placement per code
  4. Draw the one-line diagram with panel schedule
  5. Present the plan as a 10-minute job briefing
example.walkthrough: A capstone is graded on integration and judgment, not just completion. At each milestone ask: 'what decision did I make here, and why this way?'

pitfalls: Scope creep — freezing the milestone list on day one protects you.
Building without documenting — you will forget your own reasoning within days.
Perfectionism on milestone 1 — get all milestones to 'working' before polishing any to 'great.'
lessons.try_it: Write your milestone list now, with a definition of done for each.

lessons.title: Capstone: Build Log & Documentation
concepts: Keep a build log: date, what you attempted, what worked, what failed, what you learned. This becomes your documentation draft.
Your README needs five sections: what it is, why it matters, how to run it, architecture decisions, and what you'd do with more time.
Screenshots and terminal transcripts beat prose for proving hands-on work. Capture evidence as you go.
Anticipate the three hardest questions about your capstone and write the answers before anyone asks.

example.code:
README SKELETON
  # Title — one-line value proposition
  ## Why — the problem this solves
  ## Quickstart — commands to run it
  ## Architecture — decisions and trade-offs
  ## Next steps — honest limitations
example.walkthrough: Documentation written after the fact reads like fiction. The build log keeps it honest — and honesty about limitations reads as seniority.

pitfalls: README as an afterthought — start it on day one, even as stubs.
Hiding limitations — naming them with a plan reads as maturity.
No reproduction steps — if they can't run it, it doesn't exist.
lessons.try_it: Create your capstone repo/directory and write the README skeleton today.

lessons.title: Capstone: Demo & Defense
concepts: Prepare a 5-minute demo: the problem, your approach, the working result, one hard decision you made. Rehearse it out loud twice.
Defense prep: for every tool and choice in your capstone, be ready to answer 'why this instead of the alternative?'
Connect each capstone decision back to bootcamp domains — this shows integrated understanding, not isolated effort.
End your demo with honest next steps. 'Here's what I'd harden for production' is the strongest closing line.

example.code:
DEMO ARC (5 min)
  0:00 — The problem (30s)
  0:30 — Your approach (60s)
  1:30 — Live working demo (120s)
  3:30 — One hard decision + trade-off (45s)
  4:15 — Next steps for production (45s)
example.walkthrough: The demo is a performance. Rehearsal is what makes it look effortless — and effortlessness reads as mastery.

pitfalls: Demoing without a fallback — have screenshots/video if live fails.
Over-running time — a tight 5 minutes beats a rambling 15.
Memorizing a script — know the beats, speak naturally.
lessons.try_it: Do a timed 5-minute dry run of your demo this week, even if the build isn't finished.

lessons.title: Ohm's Law and Power
concepts: Ohm's law (V = I × R) is the foundation: voltage pushes, resistance opposes, current is the result — every calculation starts here.
Power (P = V × I) tells you the work rate: watts are what you pay for and what heats wires — size everything from power.
The power wheel: given any two of V, I, R, P, you can find the other two — memorize the wheel, not twelve formulas.
AC vs DC: apprenticeship exams focus on AC — voltage and current alternate direction 60 times per second (60 Hz) in North America.

example.code:
POWER WHEEL DRILL
  Given: 120V circuit, 12A load
  P = V × I = 120 × 12 = 1440W
  R = V / I = 120 / 12 = 10 ohms
  Two knowns → two unknowns. The wheel never fails.
example.walkthrough: On the exam, write the power wheel from memory first thing — it's your calculator for the whole test.

pitfalls: Mixing up V=IR variants — draw the wheel; don't trust memory under pressure.
Forgetting units — 1440 means nothing; 1440W means everything.
DC formulas on AC problems — same wheel, but watch for power factor on motor loads.
lessons.try_it: Solve: 240V, 30A circuit. Find P and R. Then find I for a 4500W load at 240V.

lessons.title: Series and Parallel Circuits
concepts: Series: one path — current is the same everywhere, voltage divides across loads, total R adds up. One break kills everything.
Parallel: multiple paths — voltage is the same across each branch, current divides, total R is less than the smallest branch.
Residential wiring is parallel: each device gets full 120V independently — that's why one lamp burning out doesn't kill the circuit.
Troubleshooting logic: series fault = everything downstream dead; parallel fault = only that branch affected.

example.code:
SERIES vs PARALLEL
  Series: 2 × 60W bulbs on 120V → each gets 60V → dim
  Parallel: 2 × 60W bulbs on 120V → each gets 120V → full brightness
  Your house is parallel. Christmas lights (old style) were series.
example.walkthrough: When a scenario describes symptoms, first ask: series or parallel behavior? It cuts the fault tree in half.

pitfalls: Adding resistances in parallel like series — parallel R always decreases.
Forgetting that series voltage divides — each load gets a share, not the full voltage.
Misdiagnosing: treating a parallel branch fault as a series fault wastes hours.
lessons.try_it: Two 100W bulbs: wire them series on 120V, then parallel. Compute each bulb's voltage in both cases.

lessons.title: AC Theory Essentials
concepts: Sine wave anatomy: AC voltage rises, peaks, falls, reverses — 60 Hz means 60 full cycles per second.
RMS values: 120V is the RMS (effective) value; peak is ~170V. Meters read RMS — the exam tests that you know the difference.
Inductive loads (motors, transformers) cause current to lag voltage — power factor drops below 1, and you pay for apparent power.
Capacitors oppose the lag: power-factor correction capacitors bring current back in phase, reducing wasted capacity.

example.code:
RMS vs PEAK
  Meter reads: 120V (RMS — the working value)
  Peak: 120 × 1.414 = 169.7V
  Peak-to-peak: 339V
  Exam trap: 'what is the peak of a 120V circuit?' → 170V, not 120V.
example.walkthrough: RMS is what does work and what the exam means by 'voltage' unless it says peak.

pitfalls: Answering 120V when asked for peak — multiply by 1.414.
Ignoring power factor on motor calcs — apparent power (VA) ≠ true power (W).
Forgetting frequency — 60 Hz is assumed; 50 Hz changes inductive reactance.
lessons.try_it: A 120V RMS sine wave: compute peak voltage and peak-to-peak. Then explain why meters read RMS.

lessons.title: Transformers and Magnetism
concepts: Transformers change voltage via magnetic induction: AC in the primary creates a fluctuating field that induces AC in the secondary.
Turns ratio = voltage ratio: 10:1 step-down turns 1200V into 120V — and steps current up inversely (power conserved).
Isolation: the primary and secondary aren't electrically connected — transformers provide safety isolation between circuits.
Pole transformers step utility voltage (7.2kV) down to residential 240/120V center-tapped — the center tap is your neutral.

example.code:
TURNS RATIO
  Primary: 7200V, 600 turns
  Secondary: 240V → turns = 600 × (240/7200) = 20 turns
  Ratio 30:1. Current steps up 30× (minus small losses).
  Power in ≈ power out — voltage and current trade.
example.walkthrough: Center-tapped secondaries give you 240V (end to end) and 120V (either end to center) — that's your house.

pitfalls: Forgetting current inverses — step down voltage = step up current; size conductors for the current.
Treating the neutral as optional — the center tap is the return path for 120V loads.
DC on transformers — transformers need changing flux; DC (steady) gives nothing out.
lessons.try_it: A 480V to 120V transformer: what's the turns ratio? If primary draws 5A, what does secondary supply?

lessons.title: Navigating the NEC
concepts: The NEC (NFPA 70) is organized by chapters: 1-4 general, 5 special occupancies, 6 special equipment, 7 special conditions, 8 communications, 9 tables/annexes.
Article 100 definitions control everything — exam questions hinge on defined terms; 'readily accessible' vs 'accessible' is a testable distinction.
The NEC is a minimum safety standard, not a design manual — it tells you what's allowed, not what's best.
Code cycle: new edition every 3 years; know which cycle your exam uses — answers change between editions.

example.code:
NEC MAP
  Ch 1: General (100 definitions, 110 requirements)
  Ch 2: Wiring & Protection (200-285)
  Ch 3: Wiring Methods (300-398)
  Ch 4: Equipment (400-490)
  Ch 9: Tables (conductor ampacity, conduit fill)
  Exam: 70% lives in Ch 1-4 + Tables.
example.walkthrough: Tab your codebook before the exam: chapters, key articles (210, 220, 250, 300, 310, 314, 334, 358), and tables.

pitfalls: Quoting remembered code instead of looking it up — the exam is open-book for a reason; verify.
Wrong cycle — a 2020 answer on a 2023 exam can be wrong.
Skipping Article 100 — definitions are the exam's favorite trap.
lessons.try_it: Look up 'readily accessible' in Article 100. Write the definition verbatim.

lessons.title: Branch Circuits (Article 210)
concepts: Branch circuit ratings: 15, 20, 30, 40, 50A standard — the rating is set by the overcurrent device.
Required circuits: small-appliance (2× 20A), laundry (1× 20A), bathroom (1× 20A) — dedicated, no other outlets.
Receptacle spacing: no point along a wall more than 6 feet from a receptacle — the 6/12 rule (6 ft from door/wall break, 12 ft max between).
AFCI protection: required in dwelling living areas (bedrooms, living rooms, etc.) — GFCI where water is near (kitchens, baths, outdoors, garages).

example.code:
DWELLING CIRCUIT MAP
  2× 20A small-appliance (kitchen/dining)
  1× 20A laundry
  1× 20A bathroom(s)
  AFCI: bedrooms, living areas, halls
  GFCI: kitchen counter, bath, garage, outdoor, crawl
  General lighting/receptacles: 15 or 20A
example.walkthrough: Draw this map from memory — it's the skeleton of every residential question.

pitfalls: Putting the fridge on small-appliance — refrigerators need individual branch circuits in practice.
AFCI/GFCI confusion — know which rooms need which (and dual-function where both).
Forgetting dedicated circuits — SABC/laundry/bath can't serve general loads.
lessons.try_it: List every required 20A circuit in a dwelling and its restrictions.

lessons.title: Grounding and Bonding (Article 250)
concepts: Grounding connects to earth (lightning, surges); bonding connects metal parts together (fault clearing) — different jobs, both in 250.
Equipment grounding conductor (EGC): the green/bare wire that carries fault current back to trip the breaker — the life-safety path.
Grounding electrode system: rod, pipe, plate, concrete-encased (ufer) — electrodes bonded together, sized per 250.66.
Main bonding jumper: connects neutral to ground at the service ONLY — downstream neutral-ground bonds create parallel paths and shock hazards.

example.code:
FAULT PATH
  Hot shorts to metal case →
  EGC carries fault current →
  low-impedance path to source →
  breaker sees massive current → trips in milliseconds
  No EGC = case sits at 120V waiting for you.
example.walkthrough: 250 is the most-tested article. Know the EGC's job cold: it's the reason breakers trip on ground faults.

pitfalls: Bonding neutral downstream — the #1 dangerous violation; single bonding point at service.
Confusing grounding with bonding — earth connection vs metal interconnection.
Undersized GEC — Table 250.66 sizes it from the service conductors.
lessons.try_it: Explain why the neutral-ground bond exists exactly once, and where.

lessons.title: Conductor Sizing and Ampacity
concepts: Ampacity comes from Table 310.16 (formerly 310.15(B)(16)) — base values adjusted for ambient temperature and conductor count.
The 90°C column is for derating math; the final ampacity can't exceed the lowest temperature-rated termination (usually 75°C or 60°C).
Derating: more than 3 current-carrying conductors in a raceway → apply Table 310.15(C)(1) factors (e.g., 4-6 conductors = 80%).
Continuous loads (3+ hours): size conductors and breakers at 125% — the wire must handle the heat over time.

example.code:
AMPACITY WORKFLOW
  1. Table 310.16 base (e.g., 12 AWG THHN = 30A @90°C)
  2. Derate: temp factor × fill factor
  3. Cap at termination rating (e.g., 75°C = 25A for 12 AWG... but 240.4(D) limits 12 AWG to 20A)
  4. Apply 125% if continuous
  Small-conductor rule 240.4(D): 14→15A, 12→20A, 10→30A max.
example.walkthrough: Work this flow on every sizing question — skipping steps is how the exam catches you.

pitfalls: Using the 90°C column directly — it's for derating start only.
Forgetting 240.4(D) small-conductor limits — they override the table.
Skipping the 125% continuous multiplier — heaters, lighting in commercial.
lessons.try_it: Size conductors for: 4 current-carrying 12 AWG THHN in conduit, 40°C ambient, continuous load.

lessons.title: Raceways: Conduit Systems
concepts: EMT (thinwall): the workhorse — lightweight steel, compression or set-screw fittings, indoor/dry locations primarily.
Rigid and IMC: heavy-duty threaded conduit for hazardous, outdoor, and physical-damage locations — costly but toughest.
PVC: nonmetallic, corrosion-proof — underground and wet locations; needs expansion fittings on long runs (it moves with temperature).
LFMC/LFNC (seal-tight): flexible liquid-tight for motors and vibrating equipment — the final connection that moves.

example.code:
CONDUIT SELECTION
  Indoor office → EMT
  Underground → PVC (or RMC where damage likely)
  Motor whip → LFMC (flex for vibration)
  Hazardous location → RMC with sealed fittings
  Match the raceway to the environment.
example.walkthrough: The exam tests selection by environment: wet, corrosive, physical damage, hazardous — each points to a raceway.

pitfalls: PVC without expansion fittings — long runs buckle; the exam loves this.
EMT in wet locations without rated fittings — standard EMT fittings aren't raintight.
Forgetting support spacing — 300.11/358.30: EMT every 10 ft, within 3 ft of boxes.
lessons.try_it: Specify the raceway for: rooftop exposed run, underground parking feed, motor connection in a washdown area.

lessons.title: Cable Assemblies
concepts: NM (Romex): dwelling wiring staple — 334 restricts it to residential, dry, not exposed to damage; the exam's favorite cable.
MC (metal-clad): commercial workhorse — armored, usable in more locations than NM, with an internal green EGC.
AC (BX): older armored cable — the armor can serve as EGC with bonding strip; know the distinction from MC.
UF: underground feeder — direct-burial rated NM-like cable; sunlight-resistant for outdoor use.

example.code:
CABLE SELECTION
  House interior walls → NM-B (334)
  Commercial office → MC (330)
  Direct burial to garage → UF (340)
  Exposed basement run → MC (NM not permitted exposed to damage)
  Environment + occupancy = cable type.
example.walkthrough: NM's restrictions (334.10/12) are exam gold: where it's allowed and — more often tested — where it's not.

pitfalls: NM in commercial — 334.12 prohibits; use MC.
NM exposed to physical damage — garages, unfinished basements: protect or use MC.
Burying NM — UF is the burial cable; NM underground fails.
lessons.try_it: For each location, name the cable: attic in dwelling, exposed run in warehouse, burial to shed, bathroom wall.

lessons.title: Boxes and Enclosures (Article 314)
concepts: Box fill (314.16): every conductor, device, clamp, and ground counts — volume in cubic inches from Table 314.16(A); overfilled boxes overheat.
Conductor count: each current-carrying conductor = 1, grounds = 1 total, devices = 2 each, internal clamps = 1.
Box support: boxes must be securely fastened — 314.23; ceiling boxes for fans must be fan-rated (50 lb).
Cover and access: boxes must remain accessible without removing building finish — burying a box is a violation.

example.code:
BOX FILL EXAMPLE
  4×12-2 NM cables into a box + 1 device
  Conductors: 8 (4 black + 4 white) = 8
  Grounds: 1 (all combined)
  Device: 2 | Clamps: 1
  Total: 12 × 2.25 cu in (12 AWG) = 27 cu in minimum
  Pick the box from Table 314.16(A).
example.walkthrough: Do box fill by the count rules, not by 'looks full' — the exam gives exact cable/device counts.

pitfalls: Forgetting device = 2 volumes — the most common box-fill error.
Grounds counted per-wire — all grounds together count as ONE.
Inaccessible boxes — 'accessible' means without damage to finish.
lessons.try_it: Compute minimum box volume: 3× 12-2 NM, 2 devices, internal clamps.

lessons.title: Devices: Switches and Receptacles
concepts: Single-pole: one location control; 3-way: two locations; 4-way: middle of 3+ location control — travelers carry the logic.
3-way wiring: power to common of one switch, travelers between, common of second to load — the exam's favorite diagram.
Receptacle wiring: line vs load on GFCI — miswired load terminals leave downstream unprotected; test buttons verify.
Tamper-resistant receptacles required in dwellings (406.12); weather-resistant + in-use covers outdoors (406.9).

example.code:
3-WAY LOGIC
  Power → common (SW1) → travelers → common (SW2) → light
  Either switch flips the traveler path → light toggles
  4-way inserts between travelers, swapping them.
  Draw it three times; the exam will show it once.
example.walkthrough: 3-way/4-way switching is pure logic — master the traveler concept and every diagram resolves.

pitfalls: 3-way with power to traveler — commons are the key terminals.
GFCI line/load reversal — downstream protection fails silently.
Forgetting TR/WR requirements — dwellings and outdoors have device rules.
lessons.try_it: Draw a 3-way circuit from memory: power at SW1, light after SW2. Label commons and travelers.

lessons.title: Motor Fundamentals
concepts: Motors convert electrical to mechanical energy; nameplate data (HP, voltage, FLA, RPM, frame, duty) drives every calculation.
Full-load current comes from Tables 430.247-250 — NOT from HP×746/V; the exam tests table use, and table values differ from theory.
Motor types: induction (workhorse), synchronous (constant speed), DC (variable speed) — each with distinct starting and control needs.
Single-phase motors need starting help (capacitor-start, split-phase); three-phase motors start themselves with rotating fields.

example.code:
NAMEPLATE READ
  5 HP, 230V, 3Ø, FLA 15.2A, 3450 RPM, 56 frame
  Branch circuit: 15.2 × 125% = 19A → 20A circuit
  Overload: 15.2 × 115% (service factor) per 430.32
  Disconnect: 15.2 × 115% per 430.110
  Tables, not theory — that's the article 430 way.
example.walkthrough: Article 430 runs on tables and percentages. Memorize the multipliers: 125% branch, 115-125% overload, 115% disconnect.

pitfalls: Computing FLA from HP — use Tables 430.247-250, always.
Forgetting service factor on overloads — 430.32 percentages key off SF.
Undersizing disconnects — 430.110 wants 115% of FLA.
lessons.try_it: From a 10 HP 460V 3Ø table FLA of 14A: size branch circuit, overload (SF 1.15), disconnect.

lessons.title: Motor Controls and Starters
concepts: Contactors switch power; overload relays protect against sustained overcurrent — the starter is contactor + overload in one.
Control circuits are typically 120V even on 480V motors — control power transformers step down for the coil circuit.
Holding circuits (seal-in): the start button energizes the coil, an auxiliary contact parallels the start button — that's why motors stay running.
Two-wire vs three-wire control: two-wire (maintained) restarts after power loss — dangerous on machinery; three-wire (momentary) requires deliberate restart.

example.code:
3-WIRE CONTROL LOGIC
  Press START → coil energizes → aux contact closes across START
  Release START → coil stays via aux (sealed)
  Press STOP → coil drops → aux opens → motor stops
  Power loss → coil drops → stays off until START pressed (safe)
example.walkthrough: Draw the seal-in circuit until it's automatic — motor control questions are ladder-logic reading tests.

pitfalls: Two-wire on dangerous machinery — auto-restart after outage injures; use three-wire.
Missing the overload in the starter — contactor alone doesn't protect the motor.
Control voltage confusion — coils are rated; match the control transformer.
lessons.try_it: Draw a 3-wire start/stop station with seal-in. Label coil, aux contact, overload contacts.

lessons.title: Overcurrent Protection for Motors
concepts: Two protections: branch-circuit (short-circuit/ground-fault) sized LARGE per 430.52 to allow starting inrush, and overload sized SMALL per 430.32 for running protection.
430.52: inverse-time breaker up to 250% of FLA for most motors — starting current (6× FLA) must not trip it.
430.32: overload at 115-125% of nameplate — protects against the slow burn of mechanical overload, not shorts.
Feeder to multiple motors: 125% of largest + sum of others (430.24) — the largest motor's starting inrush sets the margin.

example.code:
PROTECTION PAIR (15.2A FLA motor)
  Branch breaker: 15.2 × 250% = 38A → next size down 35A (430.52)
  Overload: 15.2 × 115% = 17.5A (430.32, SF 1.15)
  Big breaker for starting, small overload for running.
  That's the whole philosophy.
example.walkthrough: The exam's favorite motor trap: sizing the branch breaker at 125% like a normal load — motors get 250% for inrush.

pitfalls: 125% branch breakers on motors — that's for conductors (430.22), not breakers.
One device for both jobs — branch and overload protections are different devices with different jobs.
Forgetting the next-size-down rule on 430.52 — calculations round per 430.52(C).
lessons.try_it: FLA 28A motor, SF 1.15: size branch-circuit breaker, overload, and conductors.

lessons.title: Variable Frequency Drives
concepts: VFDs control motor speed by varying frequency AND voltage together (V/Hz ratio) — slow the frequency, lower the voltage proportionally.
Affinity laws for fans/pumps: power varies with the CUBE of speed — 80% speed uses ~51% power. VFDs pay for themselves on variable loads.
Harmonics: VFD rectifiers distort the supply — line reactors or filters protect upstream equipment; the exam tests awareness.
Bypass and disconnect: VFDs need line-side disconnecting means; bypass contactors allow across-the-line running if the drive fails.

example.code:
AFFINITY LAW PAYOFF
  Fan at 100% speed: 10 HP
  Fan at 80% speed: 10 × 0.8³ = 5.1 HP
  Energy saved: ~49% — the VFD business case in one line.
  That's why every variable-torque load gets a drive.
example.walkthrough: When a scenario mentions fans, pumps, or variable loads, think VFD + affinity laws immediately.

pitfalls: Varying frequency without voltage — motor saturates or starves; V/Hz stays constant.
Ignoring harmonics — drives pollute the supply; mitigation is part of the design.
No bypass on critical loads — drive failure shouldn't stop the process.
lessons.try_it: A 20 HP fan runs at 70% speed on a VFD. Compute the approximate power draw.

lessons.title: Shock, Arc Flash, and Approach Boundaries
concepts: Shock kills by current through the body: ~10mA can't-let-go, ~30mA respiratory paralysis, ~100mA fibrillation — voltage drives it, current does it.
Arc flash: explosive energy release from faults — incident energy in cal/cm² determines PPE category; the label on the equipment tells you.
Approach boundaries (NFPA 70E): limited, restricted, prohibited — each closer boundary demands higher qualification and protection.
De-energized work is the rule: 70E's hierarchy puts elimination first — live work requires justification, planning, and protection.

example.code:
SHOCK MATH
  120V ÷ 1000Ω (wet skin) = 120mA → lethal range
  120V ÷ 100,000Ω (dry skin) = 1.2mA → tingle
  Same voltage, 100× different current.
  Skin resistance is the variable — never trust dry conditions.
example.walkthrough: Respect the boundaries and the labels — they're written in other people's injuries.

pitfalls: 'Low voltage is safe' — 120V kills more people than high voltage through complacency.
Ignoring arc-flash labels — the cal rating picks your PPE, not your comfort.
Rushing live troubleshooting — de-energize, LOTO, verify, then work.
lessons.try_it: Look up your panel's arc-flash label (or a photo). What PPE category does it require?

lessons.title: Lockout/Tagout (LOTO)
concepts: LOTO (29 CFR 1910.147 / NFPA 70E 120): isolate every energy source, apply your personal lock, verify zero energy — your lock, your life.
Stored energy kills after lockout: discharge capacitors, block springs, bleed pneumatics — verify, don't assume.
Try-before-you-touch: after lockout, attempt start and test for voltage — the verification step catches the missed disconnect.
Group lockout: each worker applies their own lock on a hasp — no one removes another's lock, ever.

example.code:
LOTO SEQUENCE
  1. Notify affected workers
  2. Identify ALL energy sources
  3. Shut down equipment
  4. Isolate (open disconnects)
  5. Apply YOUR lock + tag
  6. Release stored energy
  7. Verify: try start + test dead
  Skip none. Ever.
example.walkthrough: Your lock is non-transferable and non-removable by others — that's the entire philosophy in one rule.

pitfalls: Locking but not verifying — the missed second source is the killer.
Sharing locks — one lock per person, no exceptions.
Forgetting stored energy — capacitors don't care about your lock.
lessons.try_it: Write the 7-step sequence from memory. Then list the stored-energy sources on one piece of equipment.

lessons.title: PPE and Insulated Tools
concepts: PPE is the last line, not the first — but when you need it, nothing else substitutes: rated gloves, eye protection, arc-rated clothing.
Insulated tools (1000V rated) for live-panel work — regular tools in a panel are a phase-to-phase short waiting to happen.
Glove classes: Class 0 (1kV) for most electrical work — inspect before each use (air test), and use leather protectors over rubber.
Test instruments: CAT ratings matter — CAT III for distribution panels; a CAT II meter on a panel can explode.

example.code:
GLOVE CHECK
  Inspect: no cuts, cracks, punctures
  Air test: roll the cuff, listen/feel for leaks
  Date: within test interval (6 months for Class 0)
  Protectors: leather outers on, always
  30 seconds that prevents a funeral.
example.walkthrough: PPE only works if it's rated, inspected, and worn — all three, every time.

pitfalls: Uninspected gloves — rubber degrades; the air test catches it.
Wrong CAT meter — panel work needs CAT III minimum.
Regular hand tools in panels — one slip, one arc flash.
lessons.try_it: Inspect a pair of gloves (or describe the air test). Check your meter's CAT rating.

lessons.title: OSHA and Jobsite Safety
concepts: OSHA 1926 Subpart K: construction electrical safety — GFCI or assured grounding on temp power; the exam tests this specifically.
Temporary power: GFCI protection on all 125V 15/20A receptacles not part of permanent wiring — no exceptions on construction sites.
Ladder safety with electricity: fiberglass ladders near electrical work — aluminum ladders and panels don't mix.
The competent person concept: OSHA requires a designated competent person who can identify hazards and stop work — know the role.

example.code:
TEMP POWER RULE
  Construction site, 125V receptacles → GFCI or assured equipment grounding program
  Extension cords: inspect daily, no daisy-chaining abuse
  Lighting: guard bulbs, no bare lamps
  The inspector checks temp power first.
example.walkthrough: Jobsite electrical safety is its own exam topic — 1926 Subpart K is short and heavily tested.

pitfalls: No GFCI on temp power — the #1 construction citation.
Aluminum ladder near panels — conductive ladders + electricity = tragedy.
Ignoring the competent person duty — someone must own hazard calls.
lessons.try_it: List the temp-power GFCI requirements from 1926.404(b)(1) in your own words.

lessons.title: Symbols and Legends
concepts: Every drawing set starts with the legend — symbols vary by engineer; never assume, always check the legend first.
Core electrical symbols: duplex receptacle (circle with two lines), switch (S with subscript), light (circle with X or fixture shape), panel (rectangle with lines).
Subscripts modify meaning: S₃ = 3-way switch, WP = weatherproof, GFI = GFCI protected — the subscript changes the device.
Reflected ceiling plans show lighting; power plans show receptacles; one-lines show distribution — know which sheet you're on.

example.code:
LEGEND DRILL
  ○ with two parallel lines = duplex receptacle
  S with subscript 3 = 3-way switch
  □ with X = luminaire
  ▭ with schedule = panelboard
  Always confirm against the sheet legend — symbols aren't universal.
example.walkthrough: The legend is sheet zero. Veterans check it on every new job; apprentices skip it and misread everything.

pitfalls: Assuming symbols are universal — they vary; the legend governs.
Ignoring subscripts — S vs S₃ is a different device and different wiring.
Wrong sheet — reading lighting from the power plan.
lessons.try_it: Find an electrical legend online. Identify 10 symbols and their subscripts.

lessons.title: One-Line Diagrams
concepts: One-lines show power distribution as single lines: service → main → feeders → panels → branch circuits — the system's skeleton.
Reading order: start at the utility/service (left/top), follow each feeder to its panel, note sizes (conduit, conductors, breakers) on each segment.
Schedules accompany one-lines: panel schedules list every breaker, load, and circuit — the one-line's detail tables.
Changes cloud: revisions are clouded and delta-numbered — always verify you're building from the latest revision.

example.code:
ONE-LINE READ
  Utility 12.47kV → XFMR 150kVA → 480V main 400A
  → Feeder 4" C, 4#500 → Panel MDP 400A
  → Feeder 2" C, 4#3/0 → Panel LP-1 225A
  Sizes shrink downstream; protection coordinates upstream.
example.walkthrough: Trace every feeder from service to final panel before pulling any wire — the one-line is the map.

pitfalls: Building from superseded revisions — check the delta and date.
Ignoring conductor/conduit notes on feeders — the sizes are the design.
Skipping schedules — the one-line without schedules is half the story.
lessons.try_it: Sketch a one-line for a small building: service, MDP, two panels, with sizes.

lessons.title: Floor Plans and Circuiting
concepts: Floor plans show device locations and homeruns: the homerun arrow points to the feeding panel with circuit numbers.
Circuit numbers (e.g., LP-1 circuits 1,3,5) tie devices to panel schedule breakers — odd/even often indicates phase on 3-phase panels.
Dashed lines = homeruns and switch legs; solid = feeders — line type carries meaning.
Dimensions and scale: verify the drawing scale before laying out — 'not to scale' (NTS) details need field measurement.

example.code:
PLAN TRACE
  Receptacle symbol → homerun arrow → 'LP-1: 1,3'
  → Panel LP-1 schedule → breakers 1,3 = 20A
  → Devices on circuits 1 and 3 identified
  Symbol → homerun → schedule → breaker. The chain.
example.walkthrough: Trace three devices from symbol to breaker. If you can't, you can't troubleshoot the building.

pitfalls: Ignoring homerun arrows — they're the only link to the panel.
Assuming scale — verify; NTS details bite.
Missing circuit numbers — without them, devices are orphans.
lessons.try_it: On a sample plan, trace two receptacles and one light to their breakers.

lessons.title: Specifications and Submittals
concepts: Specs (Division 26) govern what drawings don't show: approved manufacturers, installation standards, testing requirements.
Hierarchy: specs override drawings on conflicts — and RFIs resolve ambiguities before they become change orders.
Submittals prove compliance: product data, shop drawings — no submittal approval, no installation (on spec jobs).
As-builts: mark changes in red during construction — the as-built set is the deliverable the owner keeps.

example.code:
CONFLICT RESOLUTION
  Drawing shows EMT; spec says RMC in that area → spec wins
  Ambiguity → RFI in writing before proceeding
  Verbal direction → confirm in writing or it didn't happen
  Paper the job; memory isn't a contract document.
example.walkthrough: When drawing and spec conflict, the spec governs — and the RFI protects you either way.

pitfalls: Building the ambiguity — RFI first, always; assumptions become your cost.
Skipping submittals — installing unapproved gear risks rip-out.
No as-builts — red-line as you go; reconstruction later is fiction.
lessons.try_it: Write an RFI for a drawing/spec conflict you invent. Keep it to 5 lines.

lessons.title: Transformer Connections
concepts: Delta-wye is the workhorse: delta primary, wye secondary gives 208Y/120V — the neutral comes from the wye point.
Delta-delta: no neutral, used for 3-phase motor loads; a ground fault on one phase can go undetected — know the risk.
Single-phase center-tapped (120/240V): the residential standard — two hots 180° apart, neutral at center.
High-leg delta (240V with 208V high leg): the B phase to neutral reads 208V — mark it orange; single-phase 120V loads must avoid it.

example.code:
CONNECTION MAP
  208Y/120V: Wye secondary, neutral = wye point
  480V delta: no neutral; corner-grounded if grounded at all
  120/240V 1Ø: center-tapped, neutral = center
  High-leg: B-phase orange, 208V to neutral — keep 120V off it
example.walkthrough: Identify the system from the voltages: 208Y/120, 480Δ, 120/240 1Ø, high-leg — each has a wiring signature.

pitfalls: 120V loads on the high leg — 208V destroys them; orange marking exists for this.
Assuming all 3-phase has a neutral — delta systems often don't.
Missing the wye point — the neutral's origin explains its behavior.
lessons.try_it: For each system (208Y/120, 480Δ, high-leg), state: neutral? voltages available? key hazard?

lessons.title: Grounding Electrode Systems
concepts: Electrodes: metal water pipe, concrete-encased (ufer), ground rod, plate, ring — 250.52 lists them; use what's present.
Water pipe + supplemental: metal water pipe electrodes always need a supplemental electrode — the pipe alone isn't enough.
Ufer (concrete-encased): 20 ft of #4 rebar or conductor in footing — the best electrode; new construction should always include it.
Rod electrodes: 8 ft driven, 25 ohms or less — or drive a second rod; the 'second rod' rule (250.53(A)(2)) is the practical compliance path.

example.code:
ELECTRODE DECISION TREE
  New construction? → Ufer in the footing (best, cheapest now)
  Metal water pipe? → Use it + add supplemental
  Existing, no ufer? → Two rods 6 ft apart (skip the 25Ω test)
  Bond them all together — one grounding electrode system.
example.walkthrough: The ufer is the exam's favorite 'best answer' — know why concrete-encased beats rods.

pitfalls: Single rod without testing — 250.53(A)(2) requires ≤25Ω or a second rod.
Skipping supplemental on water pipe — the code explicitly requires it.
Separate electrodes not bonded — all electrodes form ONE system.
lessons.try_it: A new slab building: specify the electrode system and cite the articles.

lessons.title: Separately Derived Systems
concepts: A transformer creates a separately derived system: new neutral-ground bond at the transformer (or first disconnect), sized per 250.30.
Why it matters: the derived system's neutral needs its own reference — without the bond, fault clearing fails on the secondary.
250.30 sizing: grounding electrode conductor from Table 250.66 based on derived phase conductors; system bonding jumper per 250.28.
Common exam setup: 480→208Y/120 transformer feeding a panel — the bond location and conductor sizes are the question.

example.code:
SDS BOND MAP
  XFMR 480Δ → 208Y/120V
  System bonding jumper at XFMR (or first disconnect)
  GEC to electrode per 250.66 (from secondary conductors)
  Neutral bonded ONCE on the derived side
  Secondary faults now clear — the bond completes the path.
example.walkthrough: Treat every transformer secondary as a new service for bonding purposes — that's the mental model.

pitfalls: No bond on the derived system — secondary ground faults can't clear.
Bonding in two places — same parallel-path hazard as services.
Undersized GEC — 250.66 keys off the derived conductors, not the primary.
lessons.try_it: Size the system bonding jumper and GEC for a 112.5 kVA 208Y/120V secondary.

lessons.title: Ground Fault Protection
concepts: Ground-fault protection of equipment (GFPE): 230.95 requires it on 1000A+ 480Y/277V services — fire protection, not personnel.
GFCI (personnel): 5mA trip — saves people. GFPE: ~1200A max trip — saves buildings. Different devices, different jobs.
Why 480Y/277V services: ground faults there can sustain arcing that 120V faults can't — the physics demands the protection.
Testing: GFPE must be tested when installed (230.95(C)) — the exam tests that you know commissioning includes the test.

example.code:
GFCI vs GFPE
  GFCI: 5mA, personnel, receptacles/circuits
  GFPE: ≤1200A, equipment/fire, big 480Y/277V services
  Same physics (current imbalance), different magnitudes and missions.
  Never confuse them on the exam.
example.walkthrough: The exam separates these precisely: personnel vs equipment, milliamps vs kiloamps.

pitfalls: Calling GFPE 'GFCI for big services' — different purpose, different scale.
Forgetting the 230.95 thresholds — 1000A+, 150V+ to ground, 480Y/277V.
Skipping the install test — 230.95(C) requires it; it's testable.
lessons.try_it: A 1200A 480Y/277V service: is GFPE required? What trip setting max? What commissioning?

lessons.title: The Troubleshooting Mindset
concepts: Half-splitting: divide the circuit in half, test the midpoint — each test eliminates half the possibilities; it's binary search for faults.
Understand normal before diagnosing abnormal: know what the meter should read at each point, then the wrong reading diagnoses itself.
One variable at a time: change one thing, retest — shotgun part-swapping hides the real fault and wastes money.
Document as you go: what you measured, where, and what it means — the log prevents retesting and proves the diagnosis.

example.code:
HALF-SPLIT EXAMPLE
  Dead receptacle, breaker ON.
  Test at panel: 120V → panel good, fault downstream.
  Test midpoint receptacle: 0V → fault in first half.
  Test quarter point: 120V → fault between quarter and midpoint.
  3 tests, fault boxed. No guessing.
example.walkthrough: Half-splitting is the master technique — it turns exponential possibilities into logarithmic tests.

pitfalls: Starting at the device — always start at the source and work outward.
Shotgun swapping — replaced parts that weren't broken prove nothing.
No documentation — the same fault gets 'diagnosed' three times.
lessons.try_it: A dead lighting circuit: write the half-split test sequence with expected readings.

lessons.title: Meter Skills
concepts: Voltage testing: measure across the load (load connected) — 0V across a good load that's energized means no power arriving.
The floating neutral: lost neutral shows ~0V neutral-ground at panel but wild voltages (60V/180V splits) at loads — recognize the signature.
Continuity with power OFF: beep-test conductors and windings — never ohms-test energized circuits.
Clamp meters: measure current without breaking the circuit — compare against nameplate FLA to spot overloads.

example.code:
LOST NEUTRAL SIGNATURE
  Panel: 120V hot-neutral (unloaded)...
  Under load: one leg 90V, other leg 150V
  Neutral-ground: several volts (should be ~0)
  Diagnosis: open neutral — loads in series across 240V, dividing by impedance.
  Dangerous: 150V destroys 120V equipment.
example.walkthrough: The lost-neutral voltage split is the exam's favorite metering scenario — recognize the seesaw.

pitfalls: Ohms on live circuits — damages meters, lies about readings.
Neutral-ground voltage ignored — it's the lost-neutral tell.
No-load voltage tests — some faults only appear under load.
lessons.try_it: Describe the meter readings for: open hot, open neutral, shorted load — each at two test points.

lessons.title: Common Fault Patterns
concepts: Open: infinite resistance, 0 current downstream — the most common fault (loose connections, broken conductors).
Short: near-zero resistance, massive current — trips breakers instantly; find the fault before resetting repeatedly.
Ground fault: hot touching grounded metal — EGC carries it, breaker trips; high-impedance grounds smolder (fire risk).
High-resistance connection: the sneaky fault — works under light load, overheats under heavy load; thermal camera or voltage-drop test finds it.

example.code:
FAULT SIGNATURES
  Open: dead downstream, full voltage at break point
  Short: tripped breaker, low ohms hot-neutral (de-energized)
  Ground fault: tripped breaker/GFCI, low ohms hot-ground
  High-R: works lightly, fails heavily, hot spot at connection
  Match the signature, name the fault.
example.walkthrough: Pattern-match first, then verify with the meter — signatures narrow, measurements confirm.

pitfalls: Resetting tripped breakers repeatedly — the breaker is telling you something; listen.
Missing high-resistance faults — they pass simple continuity but fail under load.
Confusing ground faults with shorts — different paths, different tests.
lessons.try_it: For each fault type, write: signature symptoms + two meter tests that confirm it.

lessons.title: Preventive Maintenance
concepts: Thermal imaging: annual IR scans of panels and connections — hot spots predict failures months ahead; the camera pays for itself.
Torque: aluminum and even copper connections loosen with thermal cycling — retorque to spec on schedule, not when they fail.
Exercise breakers: rarely-operated breakers can seize — annual exercise keeps mechanisms free.
Record everything: trending IR images and torque records turn maintenance from reactive to predictive.

example.code:
PM SCHEDULE (commercial)
  Monthly: visual inspection, unusual sounds/smells
  Quarterly: thermal scan of loaded panels
  Annually: torque critical connections, exercise breakers, test GFCI/AFCI
  Records: file every reading — trends beat snapshots.
example.walkthrough: PM is the apprentice-to-journeyman differentiator: fixers react, professionals prevent.

pitfalls: IR without load — scans need operating current to show hot spots.
Over-torquing — stripped lugs are worse than loose ones; use a torque tool.
No records — unrecorded maintenance didn't happen (for the next troubleshooter).
lessons.try_it: Draft a one-page PM checklist for a small commercial panel.

lessons.title: Lighting Fundamentals
concepts: Lumens measure light output; watts measure power in — efficacy (lumens/watt) is what matters; LEDs deliver 100+ lm/W vs incandescent's 15.
Color temperature (Kelvin): 2700K warm (residential), 4000K neutral (office), 5000K daylight (industrial) — match the space's purpose.
CRI (color rendering index): 80+ for offices, 90+ where color matters (retail, medical) — cheap LEDs lie about CRI; spec it.
Lighting power density (W/sq ft): energy codes (IECC/ASHRAE 90.1) cap it — the exam tests that lighting is an energy calculation too.

example.code:
LAMP COMPARISON (800 lumens)
  Incandescent: 60W, 2700K, CRI 100, 1000 hrs
  CFL: 14W, 2700K, CRI 80, 8000 hrs
  LED: 9W, 2700-5000K, CRI 80-95, 25000 hrs
  Same light, 1/7th the power, 25× the life.
example.walkthrough: When a scenario gives lamp options, compare on lumens, CRI, and life — not just watts.

pitfalls: Watts as brightness — lumens are brightness; watts are cost.
Ignoring CRI — gray-looking merchandise kills retail sales.
Wrong color temp — 5000K in a bedroom feels like an interrogation.
lessons.try_it: Spec lamps for: living room, office, parking lot — lumens, CCT, CRI each.

lessons.title: Lighting Controls (Title 24 / IECC)
concepts: Occupancy/vacancy sensors: auto-on/auto-off (occupancy) or manual-on/auto-off (vacancy) — vacancy saves more (no false triggers).
Daylight harvesting: photosensors dim electric light near windows — the exam's favorite energy-control question.
Time scheduling: after-hours shutoff with override — required by energy codes in commercial spaces.
Title 24 (CA) / IECC: multi-level controls, shutoff, and daylight zones are code — lighting controls are as testable as wiring.

example.code:
CONTROL LAYERS (office)
  Occupancy sensor: lights off when empty
  Daylight sensor: dim perimeter to 50% near windows
  Time clock: all off 10 PM–6 AM, override at door
  Manual: dimmer at each workstation
  Four layers, each saving independently.
example.walkthrough: Energy-code lighting questions are free points if you know the control types — memorize the four layers.

pitfalls: Occupancy vs vacancy confusion — vacancy (manual-on) is the stricter saver.
Forgetting daylight zones — perimeter rows are controlled separately.
No shutoff strategy — codes require automatic off; design it.
lessons.try_it: Design controls for a 2000 sq ft office: sensor types, zones, and code justifications.

lessons.title: Emergency and Egress Lighting
concepts: Egress lighting: 1 foot-candle average along the path of egress (NFPA 101 / IBC) — people must see to escape.
Emergency power: 90 minutes minimum battery backup (UL 924) — monthly 30-second tests, annual 90-minute tests.
Exit signs: illuminated at all times the building is occupied — LED exit signs sip power; test them like emergency lights.
Wiring: emergency circuits can't share raceways/boxes with normal power (700.10) — separation is the rule.

example.code:
EGRESS CHECKLIST
  ☐ 1 fc avg on egress path
  ☐ 90-min battery (tested annually)
  ☐ Exit signs lit when occupied
  ☐ Emergency circuits separated (700.10)
  ☐ Monthly 30-sec test logged
  Life safety — no shortcuts.
example.walkthrough: Article 700 is life safety — the exam treats it with matching seriousness.

pitfalls: Normal/emergency in one raceway — 700.10 prohibits; separate them.
Skipping the 90-minute test — annual, documented, non-negotiable.
Exit signs on switched circuits — they must stay lit when occupied.
lessons.try_it: Audit a building's egress lighting against the checklist. Write up deficiencies.

lessons.title: Dimming Systems
concepts: Phase-cut dimming (TRIAC/ELV): legacy for incandescent; LED compatibility is the minefield — match dimmer to driver type.
0-10V dimming: commercial standard — separate low-voltage control pair; dimmer sinks current to set level.
DALI/DMX: digital addressable — per-fixture control and feedback; the commissioning-heavy option for complex scenes.
Flicker: incompatible dimmer/driver pairs flicker or pop — always verify the manufacturer's compatibility list.

example.code:
DIMMER MATCHING
  LED retrofit + old TRIAC dimmer → flicker risk: check compatibility list
  New commercial → 0-10V drivers + 0-10V dimmers
  Theater/architectural → DALI for addressability
  Rule: dimmer and driver must be listed as compatible.
example.walkthrough: Dimming questions are compatibility questions — the answer is always 'check the manufacturer's list.'

pitfalls: Any dimmer with any LED — the #1 callback generator in lighting.
Forgetting the 0-10V pair — it's Class 2 low-voltage, separate from line.
No compatibility check — the list exists because physics varies.
lessons.try_it: A client has flickering LED retrofits on old dimmers. Write the diagnosis and fix.

lessons.title: Jobsite Roles and Communication: The Chain of Command
concepts: The chain runs apprentice to journeyman to foreman to superintendent: instructions flow down, questions flow up, and skipping levels creates confusion plus safety risk — always work through your direct journeyman first.
Your journeyman is your primary teacher and your safety net: never freelance beyond what you have been shown, and 'I was not sure, so I stopped' is always an acceptable sentence on a jobsite.
Repeat back critical instructions — circuit numbers, voltages, lockout points — because a misheard number becomes a miswired circuit; write down anything you cannot hold in memory.

Respect the ticket: apprentices perform apprentice-level work under supervision, and doing journeyman-level work unsupervised is not ambition — it is a liability exposure and a licensing violation in many jurisdictions.

example.code:
REPEAT-BACK (example)
  Foreman: 'Kill circuit 14 in panel B before you open that box.'
  You:     'Killing circuit 14 in panel B, then I will test before touching.'
  Foreman: 'Correct.'
  The loop takes five seconds and has prevented more accidents than any tool in the bag.
example.walkthrough: That five-second loop is the cheapest safety device on the jobsite: it converts a heard instruction into a confirmed instruction, and the foreman's 'correct' is your license to proceed.

pitfalls: Nodding along to instructions you only half-heard — the repeat-back exists precisely for this.
Going around your journeyman to the foreman with questions — it undermines the person responsible for your safety.
Treating 'apprentice work' as beneath you — the ticket system protects you while you are still learning what you do not know.
lessons.try_it: Write out your own repeat-back script for a lockout instruction. Practice saying it until it feels automatic.

lessons.title: The Apprentice's Toolbelt: Hand Tools and Their Care
concepts: The starter set covers 90 percent of apprentice tasks: lineman's pliers, needle-nose pliers, wire strippers, insulated screwdrivers, torpedo level, tape measure, non-contact voltage tester, and a CAT-rated multimeter — buy quality once instead of cheap twice.

Tool care is safety: keep cutting edges clean and sharp, never use pliers as a hammer, and store insulated tools so the insulation never gets nicked — damaged insulation is invisible until the moment it fails.

The borrowing rule builds your reputation before your skill does: ask before borrowing, return it cleaner than you received it, and replace anything you break — crews remember tool borrowers long after they forget test scores.
Power tools demand the same respect as live circuits: eye protection always, workpieces secured, guards never defeated — a spinning bit does not care that you are in a hurry.

example.code:
STARTER TOOL CHECKLIST
  [ ] Lineman's pliers (9-inch)        [ ] Non-contact voltage tester
  [ ] Needle-nose pliers                 [ ] Multimeter (CAT III 600V min)
  [ ] Wire strippers (10-18 AWG)          [ ] Torpedo level
  [ ] Insulated screwdriver set          [ ] Tape measure (25 ft)
  Inspect monthly: nicks in insulation, loose jaws, cracked handles.
example.walkthrough: The CAT rating on the meter is the line that matters most: a CAT III 600V meter is built to survive transients on distribution circuits, while an unrated meter can become the fault. Match the rating to the environment.

pitfalls: Buying the cheapest meter on the shelf — an unrated meter on a live panel is a hazard, not a bargain.
Lending tools you cannot afford to lose — the borrower rule cuts both ways.
Skipping the monthly inspection — insulation damage announces itself only at failure.
lessons.try_it: Inventory your current tools against the checklist. Note every gap and every item due for inspection.

lessons.title: Documenting Your Apprenticeship: Hours, Evaluations, Advancement
concepts: OJT hours are currency: log every hour the day you work it — date, tasks performed, supervisor signature — because reconstructed logs get questioned at licensing time and questioned logs delay your exam eligibility.

Evaluations compound: quarterly reviews with your journeyman and foreman are where advancement is actually decided, so ask directly what 'ready for the next year' looks like in concrete, observable behaviors.
Classroom hours count too: apprenticeship pairs field hours with related instruction, and falling behind on classwork can hold your year back no matter how skilled your hands have become.
The paper trail protects you: documented hours, signed evaluations, and certificates are what the licensing board sees — the board never meets you, so your records are your entire reputation with it.

example.code:
SAMPLE LOG ENTRY
  Date: 2026-10-05 | Hours: 8.0 | Supervisor: J. Rivera (sig)
  Tasks: Pulled 12 AWG homeruns, set 4 device boxes, torqued panel terminations
  Related instruction: Ch. 3 — Ohm's law problem set (2 hrs)
  One line per day, every day. Gaps invite questions you do not want.
example.walkthrough: The supervisor signature is what converts your notes into evidence: an unsigned log is a diary, a signed log is a record. Get the signature the same day — memories and supervisors both move on.

pitfalls: Batching a month of hours from memory — the board can spot reconstruction, and it reads as dishonesty.
Skipping related instruction because field work feels more real — the classroom hours are a licensing requirement, not a suggestion.
Never asking for feedback until review day — by then the evaluation is already written.
lessons.try_it: Start your log today, even if your apprenticeship has not formally begun. Backfill the last week from memory, then keep it daily.

lessons.title: The Service-to-Load System: Tracing Power from Utility to Outlet
concepts: Power flows one way through a fixed chain: utility transformer to service drop or lateral, to meter, to service disconnect, to panelboard, through the branch-circuit breaker, along the branch wiring, to the device — and every handoff in that chain has protection logic and disconnect logic.

Each stage answers three questions: what protects it (the overcurrent device), what disconnects it (the disconnecting means), and what its ratings are (voltage and ampacity) — if you cannot answer all three for a stage, you do not understand that stage yet.
Troubleshooting is tracing: a dead receptacle means walking the chain backward from the load until you find voltage, and the fault sits at the first handoff where the voltage you expect is missing.

System thinking beats component thinking: a tripping breaker is rarely 'a bad breaker' — it is the protection stage correctly reporting a problem downstream, and replacing the reporter never fixes the report.

example.code:
TRACE MAP (dead receptacle)
  Device dead? -> check terminals (0V? go upstream)
  -> last device upstream on the branch (voltage here? fault between)
  -> breaker terminal in panel (120V? branch wiring fault : breaker/panel issue)
  -> service disconnect (voltage? utility vs premises problem)
  The fault is always at the first handoff where expected voltage is missing.
example.walkthrough: That last line is the whole diagnostic method in one sentence: you are not hunting the fault, you are hunting the boundary between 'voltage present' and 'voltage missing' — the fault lives exactly on that boundary.

pitfalls: Starting at the panel for every problem — start at the load and walk backward; it halves the search each step.
Replacing the breaker first — the protection stage is the messenger, and shooting it is the classic apprentice error.
Testing without a plan — random meter probes produce random conclusions; the chain gives the order.
lessons.try_it: Draw the full service-to-load chain for a house you know. Label each stage's protection, disconnect, and ratings.

lessons.title: Fault Paths: How Short Circuits and Ground Faults Travel
concepts: Normal current travels the intended loop — out on the hot, back on the neutral — while fault current takes the unintended shortcut: hot-to-neutral is a short circuit, hot-to-ground (or to a metal part) is a ground fault, and the system's entire job is to give that fault current a low-impedance path home so the breaker trips fast.

The equipment grounding conductor is the fault highway: it bonds every metal part back to the service neutral through the main bonding jumper, turning a ground fault into a high-current event the breaker can see — without it, the fault just sits there energizing the frame.

Impedance is the enemy of clearing: every loose termination and every extra foot of run adds impedance, which slows the trip and lets the fault cook — this is the physical reason torqued terminations and the single bonding point are code, not preference.

Ground faults and short circuits differ in hazard: a ground fault energizes touchable metal (shock hazard to people), while a short circuit stays inside conductors (arc and fire hazard) — the protection response is the same breaker, but your diagnostic urgency differs.

example.code:
FAULT PATH (ground fault on a machine frame)
  Hot faults to frame -> frame bonded via EGC -> EGC to panel ground bar
  -> main bonding jumper -> service neutral -> back to source
  High current (hundreds of amps) -> breaker trips in milliseconds.
  Break the path anywhere (loose EGC, missing bond) and the frame stays live.
example.walkthrough: Read that path again and notice the single point of failure logic: the whole clearing scheme depends on conductor continuity and one bonding jumper — which is why ground-impedance testing and bonding inspections are not paperwork, they are the system.

pitfalls: Thinking the ground rod clears faults — earth is a terrible fault path; the EGC-to-neutral path is what trips the breaker.
Adding a second neutral-ground bond 'for safety' — it creates parallel neutral current on grounding paths instead of improving anything.
Treating a ground fault like a nuisance trip — an energized frame is a shock hazard wearing a tripped-breaker costume.
lessons.try_it: Trace the fault path for a ground fault in a subpanel-fed machine. Mark every conductor and connection the fault current crosses.

lessons.title: Exam Strategy: The Journeyman Test as a Game
concepts: The journeyman exam is open-book and scored around 70 percent to pass: it rewards lookup speed, calculation discipline, and triage — not memorization. Treat it as a game with known rules, not a memory contest.

Question types repeat: code lookups (find the article), calculations (apply the formula), and judgment calls (pick the compliant method). Each type has its own optimal tactic, and mixing them up wastes time.
The exam is won in the margins: the difference between pass and fail is usually a handful of questions, which means time management and educated guessing are scored skills, not consolation prizes.
Know your test center's rules cold before exam day: what Code edition, what references are allowed, whether tabs are permitted, how breaks work — surprises on exam day cost points.

example.code:
THE GAME BOARD
  80 questions / 4 hours  ->  3 minutes per question
  Pass mark ~70%        ->  you can miss ~24 and still pass
  Open book             ->  lookup speed is a scored skill
  No penalty guessing   ->  blanks are the only guaranteed zeros
  Play the board, not your anxiety.
example.walkthrough: That 'miss 24 and pass' line is the psychological key: you do not need perfection, you need 56 correct. Every tactic in this domain serves that number — triage the hard ones, bank the easy ones, guess the rest intelligently.

pitfalls: Studying as if it were closed-book — memorizing article numbers instead of practicing lookups.
Ignoring the test-center rules until exam morning — a prohibited tab or missing ID can end the day before it starts.
Aiming for 100 percent — perfectionism on hard questions starves the easy ones.
lessons.try_it: Look up your jurisdiction's exam specs tonight: question count, time, Code edition, pass mark. Write the numbers down.

lessons.title: Time Management: The Three-Pass Method
concepts: Pass 1 (fast): answer everything you know in under a minute — definitions, familiar lookups, easy math. Mark everything else and move on without guilt; pass 1 banks the floor of your score.
Pass 2 (work): return to marked questions needing calculations and Code lookups, working them with full method — this is where the 125 percent reflexes and tabbed tables earn their keep.
Pass 3 (fight): spend remaining time on the hardest questions, then eliminate-and-guess any remaining blanks — pass 3 is triage, not heroics.
The 30-second rule governs pass 1: if a question needs a table, a calculation, or a long lookup, it is a pass-2 question by definition — mark it within 30 seconds and keep moving.

example.code:
THREE-PASS TIMELINE (240 min)
  Pass 1: 0:00-1:20   bank the easy (~40 questions)
  Pass 2: 1:20-3:10   work the marked (calculations, lookups)
  Pass 3: 3:10-4:00   fight the hard, guess the blanks
  Halftime check at 2:00 — behind? tighten the 30-second rule.
example.walkthrough: The timeline is a plan, not a prison — but deviations must be deliberate. The halftime check is the control: if you are behind at 2:00, the fix is stricter mark-and-move, never panic-speed.

pitfalls: Doing questions in order like homework — the exam rewards triage, not sequence.
Spending pass-1 time on pass-2 questions — the 30-second rule exists to prevent exactly this.
Skipping the halftime check — you cannot adjust a pace you never measure.
lessons.try_it: Take a 20-question practice set with a 60-minute timer. Run the three passes and log where each question landed.

lessons.title: Calculation Shortcuts: Formula Triangles and Unit Tricks
concepts: The formula triangles compress the exam's math: cover the unknown in the P-I-E triangle (P=IxE) or the E-I-R triangle (E=IxR) and the remaining two show the operation — multiplication side by side, division when stacked.
Three-phase power needs the root-3 reflex: P = E x I x 1.732 x PF for three-phase versus P = E x I x PF for single-phase — forgetting the 1.732 is the most common calculation error on the exam.

VA versus watts is a units discipline: size conductors, transformers, and services from apparent power (VA), and never mix the two — when power factor is given, true power is VA x PF, and the exam will punish conflation.
The 125 percent continuous reflex: see the word 'continuous' and multiply by 1.25 before sizing anything — make it automatic, because the exam plants 'continuous' in stems the way it plants NOT.

example.code:
TRIANGLE DRILL
  P-I-E:  cover P -> I x E ; cover I -> P / E ; cover E -> P / I
  E-I-R:  cover E -> I x R ; cover I -> E / R ; cover R -> E / I
  3-phase: P = 1.732 x E x I x PF   (line-to-line volts)
  Continuous: x 1.25, always, first.
example.walkthrough: Drill these until they are muscle memory: the exam's calculation questions are designed to be solved in under two minutes by candidates with reflexes, and to consume five minutes from candidates who derive everything from scratch.

pitfalls: Deriving every formula from first principles on exam day — reflexes are faster and less error-prone.
Forgetting the 1.732 on three-phase questions — the single most expensive arithmetic slip.
Sizing from watts when the question gives VA — or the reverse; the units must match the sizing rule.
lessons.try_it: Do ten mixed calculations — single-phase, three-phase, continuous — with a 90-second timer each. Log every unit error.

lessons.title: Code Lookup Speed: Tabs, Index, and Keyword Search
concepts: Tab the high-yield articles before exam day: 110, 210, 220, 230, 240, 250, 300, 310, 314, 334, 344, 358, 400, 404, 406, 410, 430, 440, 450, 680, 690 — these carry the overwhelming majority of journeyman questions.

The lookup hierarchy: tabbed article gets you to the neighborhood, the index gets you to the exact address — for 'which locations' and 'what is required' questions, the index is faster than any amount of article scanning.

Read the section, not just the sentence: exceptions and fine print reverse answers, and exam writers love keying the correct choice to the exception — always check for 'Exception' below the rule you found.
Keyword traps: the stem's wording often mirrors the Code's wording, so search the index for the stem's nouns first — 'receptacle,' 'arc-fault,' 'grounding electrode' — before improvising synonyms.

example.code:
LOOKUP DRILL (do 20)
  1. Read the stem; circle the nouns.
  2. Index -> article.section (one hit).
  3. Read the section INCLUDING exceptions.
  4. Match the choice to the exact language.
  Target: under 90 seconds per lookup.
example.walkthrough: Step 3 is where exams are passed: the candidate who stops at the rule gets the distractor keyed to the rule, while the candidate who reads the exception gets the answer keyed to the exception. The extra fifteen seconds are the cheapest points on the test.

pitfalls: Flipping pages hoping to recognize the answer — recognition is slower and less reliable than index-first lookup.
Stopping at the rule and skipping the exception — the exam's favorite trap.
Tabbing every article — twenty sharp tabs beat sixty vague ones.
lessons.try_it: Tab your Code tonight with the high-yield list. Then time yourself on five lookups from old practice questions.

lessons.title: Question Triage: What to Answer, Skip, and Return To
concepts: Answer now: definitions you know, lookups under 60 seconds, calculations with a ready reflex — these are pass-1 questions, and every one banked early funds the harder work later.
Mark and return: multi-step calculations, unfamiliar articles, questions with long stems — these are pass-2 questions; marking is not quitting, it is scheduling.
Fight last: the genuinely hard questions get pass 3, where you spend remaining time plus elimination guessing — a hard question deserves effort only after the easy points are safe.
Never blank: on a no-penalty exam, an unanswered question is the only answer with a zero percent chance — eliminate one choice and guess, because expected value favors the attempt every time.

example.code:
TRIAGE CARD (tape to your desk on exam day)
  < 60 sec, know it      -> ANSWER
  needs table/math       -> MARK (pass 2)
  long stem, unfamiliar   -> MARK (pass 2)
  genuinely hard          -> FIGHT (pass 3)
  time expiring           -> ELIMINATE + GUESS
  blank                   -> NEVER
example.walkthrough: That card is the whole domain on one slip of paper: the exam does not test whether you can answer the hardest question, it tests whether you can allocate four hours across eighty questions without leaving points on the table.

pitfalls: Treating marked questions as failures — marking is the tactic working as designed.
Heroics on question 12 while questions 60-80 sit blank — the hardest question is worth exactly one point, like the easiest.
Leaving blanks 'to avoid guessing wrong' — there is no penalty, so the fear is pure loss.
lessons.try_it: Take a practice exam and triage every question into the five card buckets before answering any. Compare with your instincts.

lessons.title: PV Basics: From Photons to DC Power
concepts: The photovoltaic effect turns light into direct current: photons knock electrons loose in silicon, and the cell's internal field sweeps them into a current — no moving parts, no fuel, just light in and DC out.

Cells build into modules, modules wire into strings: series connections add voltage while current stays constant, parallel connections add current while voltage stays constant — string design is voltage arithmetic against the inverter's limits.
Shade is the series string's enemy: one shaded module throttles the entire string's current, which is why site surveys obsess over chimneys, vents, and trees before a single rail is mounted.

The IV curve is the module's fingerprint: current stays flat as voltage rises until the knee, then collapses — the inverter's maximum power point tracker (MPPT) hunts that knee continuously as light and temperature change.

example.code:
STRING ARITHMETIC (example)
  10 modules, Vmp 33V each, Imp 10A each — all in series:
  String Vmp = 10 x 33V = 330V DC
  String Imp = 10A (series: current constant)
  String power = 330V x 10A = 3,300W
  Now check: Voc-cold < inverter max? (690.7) Vmp-hot > inverter min?
example.walkthrough: Those two checks at the end are the whole design discipline in one line: the string's voltage must stay inside the inverter's window at both temperature extremes — too high on a cold morning damages the inverter, too low on a hot afternoon starves it.

pitfalls: Adding currents in series — series adds voltage; parallel adds current. Mixing them up breaks every string calculation.
Designing for standard test conditions only — the field gives you cold mornings and hot afternoons, not the lab.
Ignoring shade because 'it is only one module' — in a string, one shaded module is a system problem.
lessons.try_it: For a 12-module string (Voc 41V, temp factor 1.12), compute the cold-maximum voltage and check it against a 600V inverter limit.

lessons.title: Inverters: String, Micro, and Hybrid
concepts: The string inverter is the classic: one box, one or two MPPT inputs, the whole array's DC funneled through it — cheapest per watt, but one shaded module or one failed connection punishes the entire string.

Microinverters put the inversion at each module: every panel gets its own MPPT and its own AC output, so shade, soiling, or failure affects one module only — at higher equipment cost and more rooftop electronics.
DC optimizers split the difference: module-level MPPT with a central string inverter, keeping the shade resilience while centralizing the actual inversion — a common residential compromise.

Hybrid inverters add battery readiness: they manage PV, battery charging, and grid interaction in one unit, and they are the default choice when storage is planned now or later — retrofitting battery capability onto a non-hybrid inverter is expensive.

example.code:
ARCHITECTURE CHOOSER
  Clean unshaded roof, tight budget  -> string inverter
  Partial shade, complex roof        -> microinverters or optimizers
  Storage now or later               -> hybrid inverter
  Rapid shutdown required (690.12)   -> module-level electronics simplify compliance
  Match the architecture to the roof, not the brochure.
example.walkthrough: That last line is the field rule: the roof's shade profile decides the architecture more than any spec sheet does — a cheap string inverter on a shaded roof is the most expensive inverter you can buy, measured in lost production.

pitfalls: Specifying by price alone — the cheapest inverter on the wrong roof loses more in production than it saved in equipment.
Forgetting rapid shutdown — 690.12 often makes the architecture decision for you on residential roofs.
Planning storage 'someday' on a non-hybrid inverter — the retrofit cost dwarfs the original savings.
lessons.try_it: Sketch three roofs — clean, chimney-shaded, and future-battery — and assign each an inverter architecture with one reason.

lessons.title: NEC Article 690: PV System Rules
concepts: Article 690 governs solar PV from module to inverter output: its core sizing rule (690.8) treats PV as a continuous source, requiring conductors and overcurrent protection at 125 percent of short-circuit current — the continuous-load reflex in PV form.

Voltage has a temperature rule (690.7): use the temperature-corrected maximum open-circuit voltage for the coldest site conditions, because cold raises Voc and an inverter fed beyond its maximum input voltage is a damaged inverter.

Disconnects and labeling are life-safety (690.13, 690.56): PV disconnects must be marked and accessible, and the system needs permanent placards showing voltages and disconnect locations — for the firefighter who meets your array at 2 AM.

Rapid shutdown (690.12) is the firefighter's rule: controlled conductors inside the array boundary must fall to 80 volts or less within 30 seconds of shutdown initiation — which is why module-level electronics dominate residential design.

example.code:
690 CHEAT SHEET
  690.7   max Voc, temperature-corrected (cold!)
  690.8   conductors + OCPD at 125% of Isc (continuous)
  690.12  rapid shutdown: 80V in 30 sec, array boundary
  690.13  PV disconnecting means, marked + accessible
  690.56  permanent labels: voltages, disconnect locations
  Five sections, most of the exam's PV questions.
example.walkthrough: That cheat sheet is the exam-day version of the article: five sections carry the overwhelming majority of PV questions, and each one maps to a physical hazard — overvoltage, overheating, shock, firefighter exposure. Learn the hazard and the section number sticks.

pitfalls: Sizing PV circuits like ordinary branch circuits — PV is continuous; the 125 percent is mandatory, not optional.
Using uncorrected Voc — the cold-morning voltage is the design voltage, not the nameplate.
Treating labels as paperwork — 690.56 labels are for the emergency responder, and inspectors fail jobs without them.
lessons.try_it: Write the five-section cheat sheet from memory, then verify against the Code. Repeat until it is automatic.

lessons.title: Battery Storage and Interconnection
concepts: Storage math starts with usable energy: nameplate capacity times depth of discharge equals what you can actually use nightly — a 10 kWh battery at 80 percent DoD delivers 8 kWh, and sizing from nameplate alone leaves the owner dark.

Power versus energy is the second discipline: kWh is how long (energy), kW is how much at once (power) — a battery can hold enough energy for the night yet still fail to start the well pump if its kW rating is too low.

Article 706 covers energy storage systems: working space, ventilation and thermal considerations, disconnecting means, and labeling — storage brings its own hazards (thermal runaway, high DC currents) and the Code treats it accordingly.

Interconnection has two legal paths: load-side connections through the 120 percent rule (705.12) or supply-side taps ahead of the main — and every interconnection needs utility permission first, because backfeeding a de-energized grid endangers line workers.

example.code:
STORAGE SIZING (example)
  Nightly need: 10 kWh usable
  Battery DoD: 80%  ->  nameplate = 10 / 0.80 = 12.5 kWh
  Peak load: 6 kW (well pump start) -> inverter/battery kW >= 6 kW
  Check both: enough ENERGY for the night, enough POWER for the surge.
  Miss either and the system fails differently — dark at 3 AM, or tripped at pump start.
example.walkthrough: That last line is the field lesson: energy failures and power failures look different to the owner but both trace to sizing only one of the two numbers. Size energy for the night, size power for the worst second.

pitfalls: Sizing from nameplate kWh — usable energy is nameplate times DoD, and the difference is a dark house.
Forgetting surge power — the well pump's starting kW dwarfs its running kW.
Interconnecting without utility approval — backfeed protection is a lineworker's life-safety issue, not a formality.
lessons.try_it: Size a battery for 8 kWh nightly usable at 90 percent DoD, with a 5 kW peak load. State nameplate kWh and minimum kW.

labs.objective: Solve ten rapid-fire circuit-math problems using Ohm's law and the power equation, verifying each answer with an independent formula.
steps: Open the drill terminal and note the given values (two of V, I, R, P) for problem 1.

Verify your answer with the second formula (e.g., if you used P = VI, check with P = I²R).
If the two answers disagree, find the arithmetic error before moving on.
Record your final answer and time for each of the ten problems.
Review your error pattern at the end: decimal slips, wrong rearrangement, or unit mix-ups.

checks.hint: Type solve with your answer; the drill confirms only when both formulas agree.
Type report to summarize your ten problems and error pattern.
